docs.text: The preface to the Persian translation of the Līlāvatī made for Akbar by his court poet Fayḍī (1587; Chapter 13) tells a story that has become famous: Bhāskara’s daughter Līlāvatī was destined by her horoscope to remain unmarried; her father set up a water-clock to mark the one auspicious moment for her wedding, but a pearl from her ornaments fell into it, the moment passed unnoticed, and Bhāskara consoled her by naming his book after her. The story appears nowhere in Bhāskara’s own works, and there is no evidence that Līlāvatī was a real person; the name may simply be an epithet (“playful, charming”) used for the addressee of the verses. The legend shows, however, the prestige of the book in the Persianate culture of the Mughal court.

docs.title: 5.5 The Bījagaṇita
docs.text: The Bījagaṇita begins, like Brahmagupta’s chapter 18, with the rules for positive and negative quantities and zero, the operations on unknowns, and surds. It then treats the pulveriser, the square-nature equation, equations in one unknown (linear and quadratic), equations in several unknowns, and equations involving products of unknowns (bhāvita). Colebrooke’s translation of 1817 made it known in Europe; an English version made from Persian by Edward Strachey had appeared in 1813 (Colebrooke 1817).

docs.title: 5.5.1 Surds
docs.text:
Bhāskara calls a quantity whose square root is to be taken a karaṇī. His rules include the rule for adding two surds, which in modern notation is

\[\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{a + b + 2\sqrt{ab}},\]

applicable when \(ab\) is a perfect square, so that the result is again a single surd; for example \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{8} = \sqrt{2 + 8 + 8} = \sqrt{18}\). He also gives rules for multiplying and dividing surds and for removing a surd from a denominator by multiplying by the “conjugate” expression, as in \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}}{a-b}\).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Quadratic equations and their two roots
docs.text:
For the quadratic equation, Bhāskara quotes the rule of Śrīdhara: multiply both sides by four times the coefficient of the square, add the square of the coefficient of the unknown, and take the square root.

Mathematical Result: Śrīdhara’s rule

Given \(ax^2 + bx = c\):

\[\begin{alignat*} {2} &\text{1. multiply both sides by $4a$:} &\qquad& 4a^2x^2 + 4abx = 4ac;\\ &\text{2. add $b^2$ to both sides:} && (2ax + b)^2 = 4ac + b^2;\\ &\text{3. take square roots:} && 2ax + b = \sqrt{4ac + b^2};\\ &\text{4. hence} && x = \frac{\sqrt{4ac + b^2} - b}{2a}. \end{alignat*}\]

This is completing the square, done so as to avoid fractions until the last step. Bhāskara knew that a quadratic equation may have two roots and discussed when both are acceptable. Quadratic problems had been solved long before in Babylon and by Euclid’s geometry, and al-Khwārizmī (c. 825) later sorted them into types with positive coefficients, each justified by a figure; the Indian rule is stated once for all cases, negative coefficients included (Plofker 2009; Katz 2009).

Two monkey problems

(1) The square of an eighth part of a troop of monkeys were playing in a grove, and twelve more were seen on a hill. How many monkeys were there? Solution. \((x/8)^2 + 12 = x\), that is \(x^2 - 64x + 768 = 0\), with roots \(x = 48\) and \(x = 16\). Both are accepted. (2) The fifth part of a troop, less three, squared, had gone into a cave, and one monkey was seen climbing a branch. How many were there? Solution. \((x/5 - 3)^2 + 1 = x\), that is \(x^2 - 55x + 250 = 0\), with roots \(x = 50\) and \(x = 5\). Bhāskara rejects the second, because then the “fifth part less three” would be negative, and “people do not approve” of a negative quantity in such a case.

Bhāskara also solves some equations of higher degree that can be reduced to quadratics by adding suitable quantities to both sides. His example \(x^4 - 2x^2 - 400x = 9999\) is solved by adding \(4x^2 + 400x + 1\) to both sides, which turns the left side into \((x^2+1)^2\) and the right into \((2x+100)^2\); this gives \(x^2 + 1 = 2x + 100\) and \(x = 11\). Check: \(11^4 - 2\cdot 121 - 4400 = 14641 - 242 - 4400 = 9999\).

docs.title: 5.5.3 Rational solutions of the square-nature equation
docs.text:
Before turning to whole-number solutions, the Indian authors gave a simple rule for rational solutions of \(Nx^2 + 1 = y^2\), stated by Bhāskara II and related to rules in Brahmagupta: choose any number \(m\), and take

\[x = \frac{2m}{m^2 - N},\qquad y = \frac{m^2 + N}{m^2 - N}.\]

A short calculation shows that these always satisfy the equation. For \(N = 8\) and \(m = 3\) the rule gives \(x = 6\), \(y = 17\), which happen to be whole numbers (\(8 \cdot 36 + 1 = 289 = 17^2\)); for \(N = 13\) and \(m = 4\) it gives \(x = \tfrac83\), \(y = \tfrac{29}{3}\), which are rational but not whole. The difficult problem, solved by the cyclic method, is to find solutions in whole numbers.

docs.title: 5.6 The Cyclic Method (Cakravāla)
docs.text:
Brahmagupta’s bhāvanā (Chapter 4) can produce solutions of \(Nx^2 + 1 = y^2\) once a suitable starting solution has been found, but it gives no guarantee that one can be found. The cyclic method supplies a systematic procedure. It is first known from verses of Jayadeva quoted by Udayadivākara in 1073, and was given its classical form by Bhāskara II in the Bījagaṇita (1150) (Plofker 2009; Selenius 1975).

Mathematical Result: The cakravāla

Suppose \(Nx^2 + k = y^2\) with whole numbers \(x\), \(y\), \(k\) (initially, for example, \(x = 1\) and \(y\) the integer nearest \(\sqrt{N}\)).

  1. Using the pulveriser, choose a positive integer \(m\) such that \((x m + y)\) is divisible by \(k\), and among such \(m\) choose the one for which \(|m^2 - N|\) is smallest.

  2. Form the new triple

    \[x' = \frac{xm + y}{|k|},\qquad y' = \frac{ym + Nx}{|k|},\qquad k' = \frac{m^2 - N}{k}.\]

    Then \(Nx'^2 + k' = y'^2\), and \(x'\), \(y'\), \(k'\) are again whole numbers.

  3. Repeat until \(k' = 1\). (If \(k'\) becomes \(-1\), \(\pm 2\) or \(\pm 4\), Brahmagupta’s rules can be used to finish at once.)

The step is a bhāvanā of the current solution with the trivial solution \((1, m)\) of \(N\cdot 1^2 + (m^2 - N) = m^2\), followed by division by \(k^2\); the choice of \(m\) makes the division exact and keeps the new \(k'\) small.

Scholarly Note: Why the new numbers are whole

Composing \((x, y, k)\) with \((1, m, m^2 - N)\) gives the triple \((xm + y,\ ym + Nx,\ k(m^2 - N))\). The rule chooses \(m\) so that \(k\) divides \(xm + y\). Then \(k\) also divides \(m^2 - N\): since \(y \equiv -xm \pmod{k}\) and \(y^2 - Nx^2 = k \equiv 0\), we have \(x^2(m^2 - N) \equiv 0 \pmod{k}\), and when \(x\) and \(k\) have no common factor this gives \(m^2 \equiv N \pmod{k}\). Finally \(ym + Nx \equiv -xm^2 + Nx = -x(m^2 - N) \equiv 0 \pmod{k}\). So all three numbers can be divided by \(k\) (and the last by \(k^2\) in total), leaving whole numbers. For \((5, 39, -4)\) with \(N = 61\) and \(m = 9\): \(45 + 39 = 84\), \(351 + 305 = 656\) and \(81 - 61 = 20\) are all divisible by 4.

Bhāskara did not prove that the process always ends with \(k = 1\); this was proved in modern times. In 1975 Clas-Olof Selenius showed that the method corresponds to a particular kind of continued-fraction expansion of \(\sqrt{N}\) and that it is, in a precise sense, an efficient one, often reaching the solution in fewer steps than the regular continued-fraction method of Euler and Lagrange (Selenius 1975).

The case \(61x^2 + 1 = y^2\)

Start from \(x=1\), \(y=8\): \(61 + 3 = 64\), so \(k = 3\). The cyclic method then runs as follows (\(m\) is the multiplier chosen at each step).

\(m\) \(x\) \(y\) \(k\) — 1 8 3 7 5 39 \(-4\) 9 21 164 \(-5\) 6 58 453 5 9 195 1523 4 7 722 5639 \(-3\) 8 3805 29718 \(-1\) 8 60158 469849 \(-3\) 7 296985 2319527 4 9 1248098 9747957 5 6 3447309 26924344 \(-5\) 9 11590025 90520989 \(-4\) 7 42912791 335159612 3 8 226153980 1766319049 1

For instance, from \((1, 8, 3)\): \(m\) must make \(8 + m\) divisible by 3, and of the candidates \(4, 7, 10, \ldots\) the value \(m=7\) makes \(|m^2 - 61| = 12\) smallest; then \(x' = (7+8)/3 = 5\), \(y' = (61 + 56)/3 = 39\), \(k' = (49 - 61)/3 = -4\), and indeed \(61\cdot 25 - 4 = 1521 = 39^2\). The final solution is \(x = 226{,}153{,}980\), \(y = 1{,}766{,}319{,}049\). Bhāskara II reaches it with fewer steps by combining the cyclic method with Brahmagupta’s special rules (for example at \(k = -4\), or by composing the solution with \(k=-1\) found at the seventh line with itself).

The short route is easily followed. After the first step of the cyclic method the triple is \((x, y, k) = (5, 39, -4)\), with \(y\) odd, and Brahmagupta’s rule for \(k = -4\) (Chapter 4) gives the answer at once:

\[X = \frac{5\cdot 39\,(39^2+1)(39^2+3)}{2} = \frac{195 \times 1522 \times 1524}{2} = 226{,}153{,}980,\] \[Y = (39^2 + 2)\left[\frac{(39^2+1)(39^2+3)}{2} - 1\right] = 1523 \times 1{,}159{,}763 = 1{,}766{,}319{,}049 .\]

Composing the seventh line of the table, \((3805, 29718, -1)\), with itself leads to the same result, since \(2\cdot 3805 \cdot 29718 = 226{,}153{,}980\).

docs.title: 5.7 Instantaneous Motion and the Sine Difference
docs.text:
In the Grahagaṇita of the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, in the chapter on true positions, Bhāskara II distinguishes the ordinary daily motion of a planet, the difference between its positions on successive days, from its “instantaneous” motion (tātkālikī gati) at a given moment. To compute the latter he uses a rule for the change in the sine: when an arc changes by a small amount, the sine changes by that amount multiplied by the cosine and divided by the radius. In modern notation,

\[R\sin(\theta + \delta) - R\sin\theta \approx \delta \cdot \frac{R\cos\theta}{R}\quad\text{for small }\delta .\]

Rules of this kind for the Moon’s velocity had already been used by Muñjāla (932) and Āryabhaṭa II. Bhāskara also remarks that at the point where the correction to the mean position (the “equation”) is greatest, the instantaneous correction to the velocity is zero (Plofker 2009).

Scholarly Note: Is this the derivative?

These rules are often described as a discovery of the derivative or of the differential calculus. That goes too far. Bhāskara’s rule is the statement, for one function, that the rate of change of the sine is proportional to the cosine—which in modern terms is \(\tfrac{d}{d\theta}\sin\theta = \cos\theta\)—and he uses it for a specific astronomical purpose. He does not define a general notion of rate of change for arbitrary quantities, does not develop rules for differentiating functions in general, and does not connect the procedure with the finding of areas. It is a significant piece of reasoning about instantaneous change, and the Kerala astronomers later developed related ideas much further; whether their work as a whole deserves the name “calculus” is a debated question, set out in Chapter 6 (Section 6.6). Bhāskara’s own rule is best described in its own terms (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 5.7.1 The “attractive power” of the earth
docs.text: In the Golādhyāya, explaining why the earth does not fall and why objects on all sides of it do not fall off, Bhāskara II says that the earth has an attractive power (ākṛṣṭi-śakti) by which it draws heavy things towards itself, so that they appear to fall. Similar ideas are found earlier, for example in Brahmagupta. The statement is sometimes presented as a discovery of gravitation five centuries before Newton. It is a qualitative explanation of why things fall towards the earth, of a kind found in several premodern traditions; it contains no law relating the force to mass and distance, and it was not connected with the motions of the planets, which Indian astronomy explained by other means.

docs.title: 5.8 Trigonometry: The Jyotpatti
docs.text:
A short section of the Golādhyāya, the Jyotpatti (“Production of sines”), explains how sine tables are constructed. It gives the rules for the sine of the sum and of the difference of two arcs, which in Indian form, with sines measured in a circle of radius \(R\), read

\[R\sin(\alpha \pm \beta) = \frac{R\sin\alpha\cdot R\cos\beta \pm R\cos\alpha\cdot R\sin\beta}{R},\]

together with the rules for half-arcs and the exact values of the sines of \(36^\circ\) and \(18^\circ\), obtained from the regular pentagon and decagon. With the sum and difference rules, a table at intervals of one degree can be built up from a few values. These rules give a geometric derivation of what are now the addition formulas of trigonometry; their use for constructing tables is explained step by step (Plofker 2009; Van Brummelen 2009).

The Golādhyāya also contains the standard rules of Indian spherical astronomy, such as the rule for the declination of the Sun and the rule for the “ascensional difference” (cara) on which the length of daylight depends. Indian astronomers derived such rules by projections and similar triangles inside the sphere rather than by spherical triangles; a worked example of this kind of reasoning is given in Chapter 9 (Section 9.11.1), and the astronomy itself in Volume 12 of this series.

docs.title: 5.8.1 A table at intervals of one degree
docs.text:
The Jyotpatti turns the sum rule into a recursion that can be followed mechanically. With the traditional radius \(R = 3438\), Bhāskara takes the sine of one degree as 60. To pass from the sine of any whole number of degrees to the next, he diminishes the sine by its 6569th part and adds ten times the cosine divided by 573 (Bhāskara II 1861; Plofker 2009). Writing \(J_n = R\sin n^\circ\) and \(K_n = R\cos n^\circ\), the rule is

\[J_{n+1} = J_n - \frac{J_n}{6569} + \frac{10\,K_n}{573}.\]

The rule is the sum rule with \(\beta = 1^\circ\), \(J_{n+1} = J_n\cos 1^\circ + K_n\sin 1^\circ\), in which the two constants have been replaced by simple fractions. For the cosine of one degree it uses \(1 - \tfrac{1}{6569}\), where the true value is \(1 - \tfrac{1}{6566}\). For the sine it uses \(\tfrac{10}{573} = 0.0174520\), where the true value is \(0.0174524\). The divisor 573 is chosen with care: it is exactly a sixth of 3438, so that \(10R/573 = 60\). The value 60 for the first sine and the constant in the rule are therefore the same approximation, \(R\sin 1^\circ \approx 60\) (more exactly 60.001).

The second step

For \(n = 1\): \(J_1 = 60\), and the cosine, from the right-triangle rule, is \(K_1 = \sqrt{3438^2 - 60^2} = 3437.476\). Then

\[J_2 = 60 - \frac{60}{6569} + \frac{10 \times 3437.476}{573} = 60 - 0.009 + 59.991 = 119.982,\]

against the modern \(3438\sin 2^\circ = 119.984\).

Carried through all 89 steps, with the cosine at each step found from the sine by the right-triangle rule, the recursion yields a table that never differs from \(3438\sin n^\circ\) by more than about \(0.04\) (Table 5.3). Āryabhaṭa’s rule of sine differences (Chapter 3) uses the sines alone, with a slightly wrong constant, and its errors grow as the table is built. Bhāskara’s recursion uses both the sine and the cosine, with constants correct to about one part in 40,000, and its errors grow only slowly, remaining below about \(0.04\) throughout.

Table 5.3. Sines at intervals of one degree from the Jyotpatti recursion (\(R = 3438\), recomputed) \(n\) Recursion \(3438\sin n^\circ\) Difference 1 60.000 60.001 \(-0.001\) 2 119.982 119.984 \(-0.003\) 5 299.635 299.641 \(-0.007\) 10 596.989 597.002 \(-0.013\) 30 1718.966 1719.000 \(-0.034\) 45 2430.993 2431.033 \(-0.040\) 60 2977.359 2977.395 \(-0.037\) 89 3437.475 3437.476 \(-0.001\)

A companion rule steps through the quadrant in the traditional intervals of \(3^\circ 45'\), using \(\tfrac{100}{1529}\) for the sine of the interval. By it the first sine is \(3438 \times 100/1529 = 224.85\). The 1861 translation adds, in a parenthesis that may be the translator’s, that the first sine is therefore not 225, as it is usually stated to be; the rule thus corrects the round value at the head of Āryabhaṭa’s table (Table 3.3), and the modern value is \(224.86\). The Jyotpatti also gives, beside the exact construction of the sine of \(36^\circ\), a simple approximation to it: the radius multiplied by 5878 and divided by 10,000. This is correct to four places (\(\sin 36^\circ = 0.58779\)) (Bhāskara II 1861).

docs.title: 5.9 After Bhāskara II: Sanskrit Mathematics to the Eighteenth Century
docs.text: Bhāskara II’s books dominated Sanskrit mathematics in northern and western India so completely that most later work took the form of commentary on them, or of astronomy written within their framework. This has made the centuries after him look empty in many histories. They were not, although their achievements were of a different kind from his. The Kerala school, which also began from Bhāskara’s books, is the subject of Chapter 6, and Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita’s Gaṇitakaumudī (1356), the last major Sanskrit arithmetic, of Chapters 8 and 10. This section follows the northern and western tradition from the sixteenth century to the eighteenth (Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 5.9.1 Commentary as a vehicle for mathematics
docs.text:
Dozens of commentaries were written on the Līlāvatī and the Bījagaṇita, and the most important of them did more than gloss the verses. Bhāskara had supplied explanations (vāsanā) for parts of his astronomy but few for his arithmetic and algebra, and it was the commentators who wrote out demonstrations (upapatti) of his rules systematically. Gaṇeśa Daivajña, of an astronomer family of Nandigrāma on the western coast, is best known for the Grahalāghava (epoch 1520), a handbook that computes planetary positions with simple algebraic approximations in place of a sine table; his Buddhivilāsinī on the Līlāvatī (1545) gives demonstrations of many of its rules. Sūryadāsa, son of the astronomer Jñānarāja, whose Siddhāntasundara is dated 1503, commented on both of Bhāskara’s mathematical books in the first half of the sixteenth century. Kṛṣṇa Daivajña, an astronomer associated with the Mughal court around 1600, wrote the Bījapallava on the Bījagaṇita, whose demonstrations of the rules of signs, the pulveriser and the square-nature equation are among the fullest in Sanskrit. M. D. Srinivas has drawn on these commentaries, among other sources, to show that Indian upapatti was a developed practice of justification, not an occasional afterthought (Srinivas 2005; Plofker 2009).

A commentary of this kind could carry new mathematics as well. The Kriyākramakarī on the Līlāvatī, begun by Śaṅkara Vāriyar and completed by Nārāyaṇa in Kerala in the mid-sixteenth century, contains much of the Kerala school’s work on infinite series, set out as comments on Bhāskara’s rules for the circle (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 5.9.2 The astronomers of Banaras
docs.text: In the seventeenth century Banaras became the main centre of Sanskrit astronomy, and its astronomer families, several of them from Maharashtra, argued vigorously about how far Bhāskara’s authority should extend. Munīśvara, son of the astronomer Raṅganātha, wrote the Marīci (1630s), a long commentary on the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, and an astronomical treatise of his own, the Siddhāntasārvabhauma (1646); he defended Bhāskara’s methods. Kamalākara, of a rival family, wrote the Siddhāntatattvaviveka (1658), which drew on Islamic astronomy and trigonometry and criticised Bhāskara on several points. Their dispute, conducted in Sanskrit verse and commentary, is one of the best-documented scientific controversies in the tradition, and it shows that the authority of a classic did not prevent argument over its content (Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 5.9.3 New material from outside
docs.text: The same period brought mathematics from outside into Sanskrit. Nityānanda translated the Persian Zīj-i Shāhjahānī as the Siddhāntasindhu, and at Jai Singh’s court Jagannātha Samrāṭ produced the Rekhāgaṇita, a Sanskrit version of Euclid’s Elements from the Arabic recension of Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī (Chapter 12). Euclid’s deductive geometry thus became available in Sanskrit only in the eighteenth century, and it had little effect on the way Sanskrit mathematics was written. Astronomical tables in Sanskrit, many of them computed for the handbooks of this period, survive in large numbers; their arithmetic is studied by Clemency Montelle and Kim Plofker (Montelle and Plofker 2018).

docs.title: 5.9.4 What the period achieved
docs.text: These centuries produced few new theorems, and the tradition did not develop the general algebraic notation or the analytic methods that were transforming European mathematics at the same time. Their achievement lay in consolidation and in justification: the classical rules were explained, demonstrated and taught; astronomical computation was made easier; and the Sanskrit tradition engaged, critically and selectively, with Islamic astronomy and Greek geometry. Much of this literature is still unedited, and David Pingree’s Census records large numbers of manuscripts of commentaries and handbooks from these centuries, many of which have never been studied (Pingree 1970). English translations by Edward Strachey (Bija Ganita, 1813, from the Persian), John Taylor (Lilawati, 1816) and H. T. Colebrooke (1817) introduced Bhāskara’s work to European readers just as the Sanskrit tradition of teaching it was beginning to give way to the colonial school (Chapters 13 and 14) (Colebrooke 1817).

docs.title: 5.10 Assessment
docs.text: Bhāskara I and Bhāskara II represent two kinds of achievement. Bhāskara I was an interpreter and teacher: his commentary preserved and explained Āryabhaṭa’s work, and his sine approximation is an elegant piece of original mathematics. Bhāskara II was a synthesiser: he gathered the arithmetic, algebra and astronomy of five centuries into works of great clarity and charm, corrected and extended them, and gave the cyclic method its classical form. His textbooks shaped the teaching of mathematics in India for seven centuries. The limits of his work are those of a synthesiser. He gave the cyclic method its classical form but did not show that it always ends; his treatment of division by zero is a symbolic convention rather than a theory; and his rule for instantaneous motion is applied to one astronomical problem, not developed into a general method. What he did more than any other author was to fix the form in which Indian mathematics was learned, and the commentaries on his books carried that form into the eighteenth century (Plofker 2009; Datta and Singh 1935).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compute \(\sin 60^\circ\) by Bhāskara I’s formula and compare with the true value.

  2. A bamboo 18 cubits high is broken by the wind, and its tip touches the ground 6 cubits from its foot. At what height is it broken?

  3. A peacock on a pillar 12 cubits high sees a snake 36 cubits away making for its hole at the foot of the pillar. If both travel equal distances, where do they meet?

  4. A lotus stands 1 cubit above the water; pushed by the wind, it submerges 3 cubits away. How deep is the water?

  5. Two bamboos 12 and 6 cubits high are joined by strings from the top of each to the foot of the other. At what height do the strings cross?

  6. Solve \(23x^2 + 1 = y^2\), starting from \(23\cdot 1^2 + 2 = 5^2\).

  7. Two monkeys sit on a tree 30 cubits high; a well is 60 cubits from its foot. One goes down and walks to the well; the other leaps up and goes straight to the well. If the distances are equal, how high was the leap?

  8. Simplify \(\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{12}\) by Bhāskara’s rule for adding surds.

Answers. (1) \(\frac{4\cdot 60\cdot 120}{40500 - 7200} = 0.86486\); true \(0.86603\). (2) \(x^2 + 36 = (18 - x)^2\) gives \(x = 8\). (3) 16 cubits from the pillar. (4) \(x^2 + 9 = (x+1)^2\) gives 4 cubits. (5) \(12 \cdot 6/18 = 4\) cubits. (6) Composing \((1, 5, 2)\) with itself gives \((10, 48, 4)\); halving gives \((5, 24)\), and \(23 \cdot 25 + 1 = 576 = 24^2\). (7) \(x = hd/(2h + d) = 30 \cdot 60/(2 \cdot 30 + 60) = 15\) cubits (Chapter 9). (8) \(\sqrt{3 + 12 + 2\cdot 6} = \sqrt{27}\).

Scholarly Note: Further reading

Shukla’s editions of Bhāskara I (1976) and Keller’s study of his commentary (2006); Colebrooke’s translation (1817) of the Līlāvatī and Bījagaṇita, and the modern translation of the Līlāvatī with notes by Patwardhan, Naimpally and Singh (2001); Selenius (1975) on the cyclic method; Plofker (2009), chapters 5–6, and chapters 8–9 on the later commentators and astronomers; Srinivas (2005) on the commentators’ demonstrations (Shukla 1976; Keller 2006; Colebrooke 1817; Patwardhan et al. 2001; Selenius 1975; Plofker 2009; Srinivas 2005).

docs.title: Chapter 6: The Kerala School: Infinite Series and Their Rationales
docs.text: Between the late fourteenth and the early seventeenth century, a succession of astronomer-mathematicians in central Kerala produced some of the most remarkable mathematics of the premodern world. Beginning with Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma (c. 1340–1425), they found infinite series for \(\pi\) and for the sine, cosine and arctangent, devised corrections that make the series for \(\pi\) converge rapidly, computed \(\pi\) to eleven decimal places, and wrote out reasoned derivations of these results. Equivalent series were found in Europe in the second half of the seventeenth century by James Gregory, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The Kerala results remained unknown outside Kerala until 1834, and their full mathematical content was established only in the twentieth century (Plofker 2009; Sarma et al. 2008; Sarma 1972).

docs.title: 6.1 The School and Its Members
docs.text:
The “Kerala school” is a modern name for a chain of teachers and pupils working in the region between the rivers Nila (Bhāratappuḻa) and Periyar in central Kerala, in the tradition of Āryabhaṭa. Most of Mādhava’s own writings are lost, and his results are known chiefly from quotations and attributions in the works of his successors. Table 6.1 lists the principal members.

Table 6.1. Principal members of the Kerala school Scholar Dates Works and contributions Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma c. 1340–1425 Veṇvāroha, Sphuṭacandrāpti and other astronomical works; the infinite series, known through his successors Parameśvara c. 1360–1455 Dṛggaṇita (1431); long series of eclipse observations; commentaries; formula for the circumradius of a cyclic quadrilateral Dāmodara 15th c. Son of Parameśvara; teacher of Nīlakaṇṭha and Jyeṣṭhadeva Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī 1444–c. 1545 Tantrasaṅgraha (1500); Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya; revised planetary model Jyeṣṭhadeva c. 1500–1610 Yuktibhāṣā (c. 1530), in Malayalam: derivations of the series Citrabhānu fl. 1530 Systems of equations in two unknowns (Ekaviṃśatipraśnottara) Śaṅkara Vāriyar c. 1500–1560 Kriyākramakarī on the Līlāvatī; Yuktidīpikā on the Tantrasaṅgraha Acyuta Piṣāraṭi c. 1550–1621 Sphuṭanirṇaya and other works; pupil of Jyeṣṭhadeva Putumana Somayājī 17th–18th c. (uncertain) Karaṇapaddhati: a computational manual using the series

The dates in the table are approximate. Those of Nīlakaṇṭha and Jyeṣṭhadeva are the conventional ones, derived from chronograms in the texts and from later tradition as collected by K. V. Sarma (Sarma 1972); taken literally they imply lives of about a century, and they should be read as marking the span within which each author is attested rather than as exact birth and death dates.

Mādhava is said to have lived in the village of Saṅgamagrāma, usually identified with Irinjalakuda near Thrissur; the identification rests on tradition, though it is plausible. His surviving works include the Veṇvāroha, a short text giving accurate positions of the Moon, and the Sphuṭacandrāpti. The series and the corrections attributed to him are quoted by Nīlakaṇṭha, Śaṅkara Vāriyar and Jyeṣṭhadeva, who name him as their source. Because the attributions come from his successors, it is not always possible to separate what Mādhava found from what they added, and historians speak of “Mādhava and his school” (Plofker 2009; Sarma 1972).

docs.title: 6.2 The Series for π
docs.text:
The basic series for the circumference of a circle is given in a verse that Śaṅkara Vāriyar quotes and attributes to Mādhava:

Attributed to Mādhava, quoted in the Kriyākramakarī and Yuktidīpikā

vyāse vāridhinihate rūpahṛte vyāsasāgarābhihate triśarādiviṣamasaṃkhyābhaktam ṛṇaṃ svaṃ pṛthak kramāt kuryāt

“The diameter multiplied by four (‘the oceans’) and divided by one: from this, subtract and add in turn the diameter multiplied by four and divided separately by the odd numbers three, five and so on.”

That is, for a circle of diameter \(d\),

\[C = 4d\left(1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} + \cdots\right), \qquad\text{or}\qquad \frac{\pi}{4} = 1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} + \cdots .\]

This is the series that James Gregory knew in 1671 in the more general form of the arctangent series, and that Leibniz published in 1682 (he had found it in 1673–74).

docs.title: 6.2.1 End-corrections
docs.text:
The series converges very slowly: after \(n\) terms the error in \(\pi/4\) is about \(1/(4n)\), so that a thousand terms give \(\pi \approx 3.1406\), correct only to two decimal places. The Kerala mathematicians knew this, and they corrected the partial sum by adding a term that approximates the rest of the series. If the sum is stopped after the term \(\mp 1/(2n-1)\), that is after \(n\) terms, they add or subtract a correction \(F_n\), with the sign of the next term. Three successively better corrections are given:

\[F_n^{(1)} = \frac{1}{4n},\qquad F_n^{(2)} = \frac{n}{4n^2+1},\qquad F_n^{(3)} = \frac{n^2+1}{4n^3+5n}.\]

With \(S_n = 1 - \tfrac13 + \cdots + \tfrac{(-1)^{n-1}}{2n-1}\), the corrected value is \(\tfrac{\pi}{4} \approx S_n + (-1)^n F_n\).

Mathematical Result: How good are the corrections?

Recomputed values of the error in \(\pi\) (that is, \(4\times\) the error in \(\pi/4\)) after \(n\) terms:

\(n\) no correction \(F^{(1)}\) \(F^{(2)}\) \(F^{(3)}\) 10 \(1.0\times 10^{-1}\) \(2.5\times10^{-4}\) \(2.4\times 10^{-6}\) \(5.2\times 10^{-8}\) 25 \(4.0\times 10^{-2}\) \(1.6\times10^{-5}\) \(2.5\times 10^{-8}\) \(9.1\times 10^{-11}\) 50 \(2.0\times 10^{-2}\) \(2.0\times10^{-6}\) \(8.0\times 10^{-10}\) \(7.2\times 10^{-13}\)

With the third correction, fifty terms give \(\pi\) correct to about twelve decimal places.

How the corrections were found is explained in the Yuktibhāṣā and the Kriyākramakarī: the authors seek a correction such that the corrected sums for \(n\) and \(n+1\) terms agree as closely as possible, and they improve it step by step.

Scholarly Note: The criterion in modern form

If the corrected value is to be the same whether one stops after \(n\) or after \(n+1\) terms, then, since the \((n+1)\)-th term is \(\pm\frac{1}{2n+1}\), the correction must satisfy

\[F(n) + F(n+1) = \frac{1}{2n+1}.\]

No simple rational function satisfies this exactly, but one can make the discrepancy small. For the three Kerala corrections the discrepancies are

\[\begin{gather*} \frac{1}{4n(n+1)(2n+1)},\qquad \frac{-4}{(2n+1)(4n^2+1)(4n^2+8n+5)},\\[4pt] \frac{9}{n(n+1)(2n+1)(4n^2+5)(4n^2+8n+9)}, \end{gather*}\]

which for large \(n\) behave like \(\frac{1}{8n^3}\), \(-\frac{1}{8n^5}\) and \(\frac{9}{32n^7}\). Each correction is thus much better than the last, which explains the rapid improvement shown in the table above. The Yuktibhāṣā carries out the equivalent reasoning in words, measuring the “grossness” (sthaulya) of each correction and seeking to reduce it.

T. Hayashi, T. Kusuba and M. Yano showed in 1990 that the three corrections are the successive approximations (convergents) of the continued fraction

\[\dfrac{1}{4n + \dfrac{1^2}{n + \dfrac{2^2}{4n + \dfrac{3^2}{n + \cdots}}}}\]

which represents the remainder of the series exactly. Whether the Kerala mathematicians saw the corrections in this way is not known (Hayashi et al. 1990; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.2.2 Faster series
docs.text:
The same sources give transformed series that converge much faster. One, attributed to Mādhava, is

\[\pi = \sqrt{12}\left(1 - \frac{1}{3\cdot 3} + \frac{1}{5\cdot 3^2} - \frac{1}{7\cdot 3^3} + \cdots\right),\]

which is the arctangent series for \(\arctan(1/\sqrt{3}) = \pi/6\). Each term is about a third of the previous one, and after 21 terms the error is less than \(10^{-11}\). Others are obtained by combining terms of the basic series in pairs, for example

\[\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{3^3 - 3} - \frac{1}{5^3 - 5} + \frac{1}{7^3 - 7} - \cdots,\]

whose terms decrease like the inverse cube.

docs.title: 6.2.3 The value of π
docs.text:
A verse attributed to Mādhava gives the circumference of a circle of diameter \(9 \times 10^{11}\) in word-numerals (bhūtasaṃkhyā):

Attributed to Mādhava

vibudhanetragajāhihutāśanatriguṇavedabhavāraṇabāhavaḥ navanikharvamite vṛtivistare paridhimānam idaṃ jagadur budhāḥ

“Gods (33), eyes (2), elephants (8), serpents (8), fires (3), three (3), qualities (3), Vedas (4), lunar mansions (27), elephants (8), arms (2): the wise have said that this is the measure of the circumference when the diameter is nine nikharva (\(9\times 10^{11}\)).”

Read from the last word to the first, the numbers give \(2\,8\,27\,4\,3\,3\,3\,8\,8\,2\,33\), that is \(2{,}827{,}433{,}388{,}233\). Hence

\[\pi \approx \frac{2{,}827{,}433{,}388{,}233}{900{,}000{,}000{,}000} = 3.14159265359\ldots,\]

correct to eleven decimal places (\(\pi = 3.14159265358979\ldots\)). This was an outstanding achievement, but not a unique one: in Samarqand the astronomer Jamshīd al-Kāshī calculated \(2\pi\) to the equivalent of sixteen decimal places in 1424, by inscribing polygons, and Mādhava’s exact date for his value is not known. In Europe Ludolph van Ceulen published \(\pi\) to 20 places in 1596, and 35 places were published after his death.

docs.title: 6.3 The Sine, Cosine and Arctangent Series
docs.text:
The Kerala texts also give series for the sine and cosine of an arc. In the Indian form, with the arc \(s\) measured in the same units as the radius \(R\), they read

\[R\sin\frac{s}{R} = s - \frac{s^3}{3!\,R^2} + \frac{s^5}{5!\,R^4} - \cdots,\qquad R - R\cos\frac{s}{R} = \frac{s^2}{2!\,R} - \frac{s^4}{4!\,R^3} + \cdots,\]

which, with \(\theta = s/R\), are the familiar

\[\sin\theta = \theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} - \cdots,\qquad \cos\theta = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} - \cdots .\]

The texts also give a series for the arc in terms of its sine and cosine, which is equivalent to the arctangent series

\[\theta = \tan\theta - \frac{\tan^3\theta}{3} + \frac{\tan^5\theta}{5} - \cdots \qquad (\text{for } |\tan\theta| \le 1),\]

and from which the series for \(\pi/4\) follows by taking \(\theta = 45^\circ\). In Europe the sine and cosine series were found by Newton (1669, published later), and the arctangent series by Gregory (1671).

For practical computation, the Kerala astronomers arranged the terms of the sine series so that they could be evaluated by repeated multiplication and division (Section 6.8), and they gave a table of sines for the 24 standard arcs, more accurate than Āryabhaṭa’s, encoded in a verse in the kaṭapayādi notation. Mādhava’s sine values are given in minutes, seconds and thirds of arc (a third being a sixtieth of a second), which corresponds roughly to seven or eight significant figures (Plofker 2009; Gold and Pingree 1991).

docs.title: 6.4.1 The text
docs.text: The Yuktibhāṣā (“Discourse on rationales”), written in Malayalam by Jyeṣṭhadeva around 1530, sets out the reasoning behind the mathematics and astronomy of Nīlakaṇṭha’s Tantrasaṅgraha. Its first part, on mathematics, explains the arithmetic operations, the “ten questions” on finding two quantities from their sum, difference, product and so on, fractions, the rule of three and the theorem of the right triangle, and then derives the series for \(\pi\), the corrections, and the sine and cosine series. Its second part treats astronomy. It is written in continuous prose and argues step by step. K. V. Sarma’s edition, with an English translation and explanatory notes by K. Ramasubramanian, M. D. Srinivas and M. S. Sriram (2008), has made it accessible to modern readers (Sarma et al. 2008). Śaṅkara Vāriyar’s Sanskrit commentaries give closely related derivations.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Polygons first
docs.text:
Before deriving the series, the Yuktibhāṣā explains how the circumference can be approached by polygons. Starting from the square inscribed in (or circumscribed about) a circle, the number of sides is doubled repeatedly, and at each stage the side of the new polygon is computed from the side of the old by the rule of the right triangle. The perimeters approach the circumference, but slowly: for inscribed polygons in a circle of diameter 1,

Sides Perimeter Sides Perimeter 4 2.8284 128 3.14128 8 3.0615 256 3.14151 16 3.1214 512 3.141573 32 3.1365 1024 3.141588 64 3.1403

Each doubling requires the extraction of a square root, and many doublings are needed for even modest accuracy. The text uses this to motivate a better method, which leads to the infinite series.

docs.title: 6.4.3 The derivation of the series for π
docs.text:
The argument for the series of \(\pi\) may be summarised as follows; Section 6.5 follows it step by step, in its general form.

  1. Consider a circle of radius \(r\) inscribed in a square, and the part of one side of the square that runs from the point where the circle touches it to the corner; its length is \(r\), and it subtends one eighth of the circumference. Divide this segment into \(n\) equal parts and join the division points to the centre. The lines cut the eighth of the circle into \(n\) small arcs.

  2. Using similar triangles, each small arc is approximately

    \[\frac{r^2\,(r/n)}{r^2 + x_k^2},\]

    where \(x_k = kr/n\) is the distance of the \(k\)-th division point from the point of contact, so that \(\sqrt{r^2 + x_k^2}\) is its distance from the centre.

  3. The fraction \(1/(r^2 + x^2)\) is expanded as a series by repeated division:

    \[\frac{1}{r^2 + x^2} = \frac{1}{r^2}\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{r^2} + \frac{x^4}{r^4} - \cdots\right).\]

  4. The resulting sums of powers \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^p\) are needed for large \(n\). Here the text uses the result, which it also derives, that for large \(n\)

    \[\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^p \approx \frac{n^{p+1}}{p+1}.\]

  5. Substituting, the eighth part of the circumference is found to be \(r\left(1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots\right)\), and the approximation becomes exact as the number of divisions grows without limit.

The step involving sums of powers is the heart of the argument. The Yuktibhāṣā derives the approximation by an argument in which each sum is obtained from the previous one, and it states explicitly that the result holds when the number of parts is so large that a single unit can be neglected in comparison with it. In modern terms, the argument is equivalent to evaluating the integral \(\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \frac{\pi}{4}\) by expanding the integrand in a series and integrating term by term, with the power sums playing the role of \(\int_0^1 x^p\,dx = \frac{1}{p+1}\). The sine and cosine series are derived by a similar method: the sines and versed sines of an arc are expressed through repeated summation of the second differences of sines (an idea going back to Āryabhaṭa, Chapter 3), and the repeated sums are again approximated by power sums (Sarma et al. 2008; Divakaran 2018).

The Yuktibhāṣā’s arguments deal explicitly with what happens when quantities become very small or very many. They are not proofs in the sense of nineteenth-century analysis, which defined limits and convergence precisely; nor were the arguments of Newton or Leibniz. Whether the method they embody should be called “calculus” is a matter of debate, taken up in Section 6.6 after the derivation has been followed in detail.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Sums of powers
docs.text:
The step on which everything depends—that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^p\) is approximately \(n^{p+1}/(p+1)\) when \(n\) is large—is itself argued in the Yuktibhāṣā by an ingenious recursion. In modern notation the idea is the following. Write \(S_p(n) = 1^p + 2^p + \cdots + n^p\). Then

\[n\,S_{p-1}(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} n\,k^{p-1} = S_p(n) + \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^{p-1}(n - k).\]

The last sum is a sum of the partial sums \(S_{p-1}(1) + S_{p-1}(2) + \cdots + S_{p-1}(n-1)\). If the rule is already known for \(p - 1\), these partial sums are approximately \(j^p/p\), and their total is approximately \(S_p(n)/p\). Hence \(n \cdot \frac{n^p}{p} \approx S_p(n)\left(1 + \frac{1}{p}\right)\), that is, \(S_p(n) \approx \frac{n^{p+1}}{p+1}\). Starting from \(S_1(n) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \approx \frac{n^2}{2}\), the rule follows for every power. The approximation improves as \(n\) grows:

\(n = 10\) \(n = 100\) \(n = 1000\) \(S_2(n) \div \dfrac{n^3}{3}\) 1.155 1.0151 1.0015 \(S_3(n) \div \dfrac{n^4}{4}\) 1.210 1.0201 1.0020

The text is explicit that the rule holds only when the number of parts is very large, so that a single part can be neglected.

docs.title: 6.4.5 The sine series
docs.text:
The derivation of the sine series uses the property of sine differences already known to Āryabhaṭa (Chapter 3): the second differences of the sines are proportional to the sines themselves. Divide an arc \(s\) (measured in units of the radius \(R\)) into \(n\) equal small parts of length \(\delta = s/n\). Summing the second differences twice expresses the sine of the arc as the arc itself diminished by a double sum of sines:

\[R\sin\frac{s}{R} \approx s - \frac{\delta^2}{R^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\ \sum_{k=1}^{j} R\sin\frac{k\delta}{R} .\]

As a first approximation, each sine inside the sum is replaced by its arc, \(k\delta\); the double sum is then about \(\delta n^3/6\), and multiplied by \(\delta^2/R^2\) it becomes \(\delta^3 n^3/(6R^2) = s^3/(6R^2)\), which gives \(R\sin(s/R) \approx s - s^3/(6R^2)\). Putting this improved value back inside the sum and using the rule for sums of powers again gives the next term, \(+\,s^5/(120R^4)\), and so on indefinitely. The Yuktibhāṣā carries out this iteration in words and arrives at the full series for the sine and the versed sine (Sarma et al. 2008; Gold and Pingree 1991).

docs.title: 6.4.6 The sum of an infinite geometric series
docs.text:
How the Kerala authors thought about a sum of endlessly many terms can be seen in a short argument in Nīlakaṇṭha’s commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya. In the course of a geometrical discussion of the circle he needs the sum

\[\frac14 + \frac{1}{4^2} + \frac{1}{4^3} + \cdots\]

and shows that it is \(\tfrac13\). In modern notation his reasoning runs as follows. Since \(\tfrac13 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac{1}{4\cdot 3}\), and likewise \(\tfrac{1}{4\cdot 3} = \tfrac{1}{4^2} + \tfrac{1}{4^2\cdot 3}\), and so on, after \(n\) steps

\[\frac13 = \frac14 + \frac{1}{4^2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{4^n} + \frac{1}{4^n\cdot 3}.\]

The partial sums \(0.25\), \(0.3125\), \(0.328125\), \(0.33203125, \ldots\) therefore always fall short of \(\tfrac13\), and the shortfall \(\tfrac{1}{3\cdot 4^n}\) is divided by four at every step (\(0.0833\), \(0.0208\), \(0.0052\), \(0.0013, \ldots\)). When it has become too small to matter, the sum of the terms may be taken as \(\tfrac13\) itself. The argument treats the value of an infinite series as the quantity that its partial sums approach as closely as one wishes, the same understanding that underlies the Yuktibhāṣā’s treatment of the series for \(\pi\) and the sine. It is stated for a particular series and justified by the explicit remainder, not by a general theory of convergence (Plofker 2009; Divakaran 2018).

docs.title: 6.5 The Arc from Its Tangent: The Derivation Step by Step
docs.text: The outline in Section 6.4 gives the shape of the Yuktibhāṣā’s argument for the series of \(\pi\). This argument is the best-documented example of how the Kerala mathematicians reasoned about very many very small quantities, so it is worth following one derivation through without skipping steps. It is set out here in the general form that gives the series for an arc in terms of its tangent, the modern arctangent series. The series for \(\pi\) is then the special case of an eighth of the circle. The figure and the sequence of steps follow the text as it is explained in the edition of Sarma, Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram. The algebraic notation and the numerical checks are modern (Sarma et al. 2008; Divakaran 2018; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.5.1 The figure
docs.text:
Let a circle of radius \(r\) have its centre at \(O\), and draw the tangent to the circle at a point \(T\) (Figure 6.1). Mark a point \(P\) on the tangent at a distance \(t\) from \(T\). The line \(OP\) cuts the circle at \(A\), and \(t\) is the tangent of the arc \(TA\). In the Indian terms of Chapter 3, if the radius is \(R\), the tangent is the sine of the arc multiplied by the radius and divided by the cosine, \(t = R\cdot\textrm{jyā}/\textrm{koṭijyā}\). For the eighth of the circle, \(P\) is the corner of the square circumscribing the circle, and \(t = r\).

Divide \(TP\) into \(n\) equal parts of length \(t/n\). Call the division points \(P_0 = T, P_1, \ldots, P_n = P\), so that \(P_i\) lies at the distance \(x_i = it/n\) from \(T\), and join each of them to the centre. The text calls these joining lines karṇas (“hypotenuses”), since each is the hypotenuse of a right triangle \(OTP_i\). Their lengths are

\[k_i = \sqrt{r^2 + x_i^2}.\]

The hypotenuses cut the arc \(TA\) into \(n\) small arcs. These are not equal: the pieces near \(T\) are larger than those near \(A\), because the distant parts of the tangent are seen from the centre at a slant.

Figure 6.1. The construction of the Yuktibhāṣā for the arc \(TA\) whose tangent is \(TP = t\), drawn for the eighth of the circle (\(t = r\)) with \(n = 4\). The perpendicular \(P_{i-1}Q\) falls on the hypotenuse \(OP_i\), and \(BC\) is the half-chord of the small arc between \(OP_{i-1}\) and \(OP_i\).

docs.title: 6.5.2 Two pairs of similar triangles
docs.text:
Take the \(i\)-th piece of the tangent, \(P_{i-1}P_i\), of length \(t/n\). From \(P_{i-1}\) drop a perpendicular onto the hypotenuse \(OP_i\), meeting it at \(Q\). The small right triangle \(P_{i-1}QP_i\) and the large right triangle \(OTP_i\) have the same angle at \(P_i\), so they are similar. Comparing corresponding sides,

\[\frac{P_{i-1}Q}{P_{i-1}P_i} = \frac{OT}{OP_i},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad P_{i-1}Q = \frac{t}{n}\cdot\frac{r}{k_i}.\]

Next, let the hypotenuse \(OP_{i-1}\) meet the circle at \(B\), and drop a perpendicular \(BC\) from \(B\) onto \(OP_i\). The right triangles \(OBC\) and \(OP_{i-1}Q\) share the angle at \(O\), so they too are similar, and

\[BC = P_{i-1}Q\cdot\frac{OB}{OP_{i-1}} = \frac{t}{n}\cdot\frac{r^2}{k_{i-1}\,k_i}.\]

The segment \(BC\) is the half-chord, that is, the Indian sine, of the small arc that lies between the two hypotenuses. Up to this point nothing has been approximated: the formula for \(BC\) is exact.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Two approximations
docs.text:
The text now makes two simplifications, each of which becomes negligible as the number of parts grows. First, a very small arc is taken as equal to its own sine, the half-chord \(BC\). Second, the product \(k_{i-1}k_i\) of two neighbouring hypotenuses is replaced by the square of one of them, since the two differ very little when the parts are small. The \(i\)-th small arc is then taken as

\[\frac{t}{n}\cdot\frac{r^2}{k_i^2} = \frac{t}{n}\cdot\frac{r^2}{r^2 + x_i^2}.\]

How quickly the two simplifications lose their effect can be checked numerically. Table 6.2 adds up the pieces for the eighth of a circle of radius 1, whose true length is \(\pi/4 = 0.785398\). The sum of the exact half-chords \(BC\) is already close for small \(n\), because replacing an arc by its sine discards an error of the order of the cube of the small angle. Replacing the product of the hypotenuses by a square leaves an error of about \(1/(4n)\), which falls tenfold with each tenfold increase in \(n\). Both errors can be made as small as one wishes, and this is all that the argument needs.

Table 6.2. The Yuktibhāṣā’s pieces summed for the eighth of a circle of radius 1 (recomputed); the true value is \(\pi/4 = 0.785398\) Parts \(n\) Sum of half-chords \(\dfrac{t}{n}\dfrac{r^2}{k_{i-1}k_i}\) Sum of \(\dfrac{t}{n}\dfrac{r^2}{k_i^2}\) 5 0.781787 0.733732 10 0.784492 0.759981 100 0.785389 0.782894 1000 0.785398 0.785148

docs.title: 6.5.4 Expanding the fraction by repeated correction
docs.text:
The pieces cannot be added as they stand, because each has the hypotenuse in its denominator. The text turns the fraction into a sum of simple terms by a procedure of repeated correction. A quantity \(a\) multiplied by \(r^2\) and divided by \(r^2 + x^2\) is first taken to be \(a\) itself. This is too large, and the excess is

\[a - a\,\frac{r^2}{r^2+x^2} = \frac{a x^2}{r^2}\cdot\frac{r^2}{r^2+x^2},\]

which is a quantity of the same form as the one we began with, with \(a\) replaced by \(a x^2/r^2\). Treating the excess in the same way, and the excess of the excess, and so on without end, gives

\[a\,\frac{r^2}{r^2+x^2} = a - a\,\frac{x^2}{r^2} + a\,\frac{x^4}{r^4} - a\,\frac{x^6}{r^6} + \cdots .\]

At each stage the part not yet accounted for is a quantity of the original form multiplied by a further factor \(x^2/r^2\). When \(x\) is less than \(r\) this remainder shrinks at every step, and the process can be stopped whenever it has become negligible. The argument is the same in kind as Nīlakaṇṭha’s treatment of the geometric series in Section 6.4, where the remainder is also written down explicitly and seen to diminish.

docs.title: 6.5.5 Summing the pieces
docs.text:
Put \(a = t/n\) and \(x = x_i = it/n\), and add the \(n\) pieces. Collecting the terms of each kind,

\[\textrm{arc}\ TA \approx t - \frac{t^3}{r^2}\cdot\frac{1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + n^2}{n^3} + \frac{t^5}{r^4}\cdot\frac{1^4 + 2^4 + \cdots + n^4}{n^5} - \cdots .\]

Each column is a sum of equal powers of the natural numbers, divided by a power of \(n\). By the rule for such sums derived in the Yuktibhāṣā itself (Section 6.4), the sum of the \(p\)-th powers up to \(n\) is close to \(n^{p+1}/(p+1)\) when \(n\) is very large. The quotients therefore become \(\tfrac13\), \(\tfrac15\), \(\tfrac17\), and so on, and

\[\textrm{arc}\ TA = t - \frac{t^3}{3r^2} + \frac{t^5}{5r^4} - \frac{t^7}{7r^6} + \cdots .\]

For the eighth of the circle, \(t = r\) and the arc is \(r\bigl(1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots\bigr)\). Eight such arcs make the circumference, so that \(C = 8r\bigl(1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots\bigr) = 4d\bigl(1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots\bigr)\), which is the rule of Section 6.2.

docs.title: 6.5.6 The rule in Indian form, and its limit
docs.text:
Written with the Indian sine and cosine, where \(t = R\cdot\textrm{jyā}/\textrm{koṭijyā}\), the result becomes

\[\textrm{arc} = R\,\frac{\textrm{jyā}}{\textrm{koṭijyā}} - \frac{R}{3}\left(\frac{\textrm{jyā}}{\textrm{koṭijyā}}\right)^{3} + \frac{R}{5}\left(\frac{\textrm{jyā}}{\textrm{koṭijyā}}\right)^{5} - \cdots .\]

This is the form in which the rule attributed to Mādhava is usually rendered. The first result is the sine multiplied by the radius and divided by the cosine. Each further result comes from the previous one by multiplying by the square of the sine and dividing by the square of the cosine. The results are divided in turn by the odd numbers \(1, 3, 5, \ldots\), and are subtracted and added alternately (Plofker 2009; Sarma et al. 2008).

The derivation also shows where the rule stops working. The repeated correction succeeds only while each remainder is smaller than the last, that is, while \(x\) is less than \(r\). For the arc, this means a tangent no greater than the radius, or a sine no greater than the cosine: an arc of at most an eighth of the circle. For a larger arc the terms grow instead of shrinking. With \(t = 2r\), for instance, they are \(2r\), \(\tfrac83 r\), \(\tfrac{32}{5}r\), \(\tfrac{128}{7}r, \ldots\) and the sum has no value. The rule as it is quoted in the Kerala texts accordingly directs that the smaller of the sine and the cosine be taken as the sine, since otherwise the computation would never come to an end; a larger arc is thus found from its complement. Conversely, the smaller the tangent, the faster the series converges. For the twelfth part of the circle (\(30^\circ\)) the tangent is \(r/\sqrt3\), and the arctangent series becomes the rapidly converging series for \(\pi\) in Section 6.2.

docs.title: 6.5.7 What the derivation shows
docs.text:
Two features of the argument deserve notice. First, every approximation is stated, and each is of a kind that disappears as the parts are made smaller: an arc is replaced by its sine, two neighbouring hypotenuses by one, and a sum of powers by its leading term. The text justifies each step by the principle that, when the parts are very many, a single part can be neglected. Second, the structure of the argument is that of a modern evaluation of the integral

\[\int_0^{t}\frac{r^2\,dx}{r^2+x^2},\]

in which the integrand is expanded in a series and integrated term by term. The resemblance is real. How much weight it should bear—whether the Yuktibhāṣā here practises the integral calculus, or carries out for one figure a procedure that the calculus later made general—is the question of the next section (Sarma et al. 2008; Divakaran 2018).

docs.title: 6.6 Was It Calculus? A Debate About Definitions
docs.text: The derivations just followed raise a question that has been asked ever since the series became known outside Kerala: did the Kerala mathematicians possess the calculus? The disagreement is partly about evidence, but mostly about what the word should be taken to mean. It is therefore best set out as a debate, with each position attributed to those who hold it.

docs.title: 6.6.1 What is agreed
docs.text: The content of the texts is not in dispute. The Yuktibhāṣā and Śaṅkara Vāriyar’s Sanskrit commentaries divide a length into \(n\) equal parts and add up the resulting small quantities; they say explicitly that the result becomes exact when \(n\) is so large that a single part may be neglected; they evaluate the sums with the rule \(\sum k^p \approx n^{p+1}/(p+1)\), which they derive; they expand a quotient into an endless series by repeated correction, with the remainder written down at each stage; and in this way they obtain the power series for the arctangent, the sine and the cosine, together with the estimates of the remainder that lead to the end-corrections. Kerala astronomers also computed instantaneous planetary velocities by rules that extend Bhāskara II’s rule for the change in the sine (Section 5.7). Nor is it disputed that the European calculus of Newton and Leibniz was reached independently, by another route (Section 6.13).

docs.title: 6.6.2 The strong reading
docs.text: P. P. Divakaran has argued that this body of work is calculus in the full sense. His article of 2007 calls the Yuktibhāṣā “the first textbook of calculus”, and his book of 2018 develops the case at length (Divakaran 2007, 2018). K. Ramasubramanian and M. D. Srinivas, two of the editors and translators of the Yuktibhāṣā, likewise describe the Kerala work as the “development of calculus in India” and stress the systematic character of its demonstrations (Ramasubramanian and Srinivas 2010; Sarma et al. 2008). Those who take this view point out that the defining moves of the integral calculus—the passage from a finite sum to a limit in which the parts become indefinitely small, the evaluation of such limits for powers, which is equivalent to \(\int_0^1 x^p\,dx = \tfrac{1}{p+1}\), and the use of these results to obtain new functions as infinite series—are all explicit in the text; that they are presented as a connected method applied to several problems, not as isolated tricks; and that the remainders are controlled, so that the results are not mere approximations.

docs.title: 6.6.3 The cautious reading
docs.text: Others keep the word “calculus” for the general discipline created in seventeenth-century Europe: a symbolic method that applies to any curve or function, with general rules for finding rates of change and areas, and the fundamental theorem that links the two. Victor Katz, comparing the Islamic and Indian material, concluded that both traditions had developed many of the ideas involved but had not combined them into such general tools (Katz 1995). Kim Plofker’s survey gives the Kerala results a central place but describes them in their own terms, as techniques worked out for the circle and its trigonometric quantities, rather than as “the calculus” (Plofker 2009). On this reading the Kerala texts apply methods of the integral calculus to particular problems, and use differential reasoning in a limited form, without possessing the calculus as a general theory.

docs.title: 6.6.4 Weighing the readings
docs.text: The two readings agree on what the texts say. They differ on whether generality, and the link between rates of change and summation, belong to the meaning of the word. The strong reading is right that the Kerala methods are more than approximations: the limits are stated, the remainders estimated and the method carried across several series. The cautious reading is right that the surviving texts do not formulate a rule for an arbitrary function, do not state the connection between their summations and the instantaneous velocities computed in the same tradition, and remain tied to the circle. Neither reading measures the Kerala achievement by a European yardstick of priority; the question is one of classification. This volume therefore describes the methods themselves in detail and uses the word “calculus” only with this qualification. The reader can judge from the derivation in Section 6.5 which description is more apt.

docs.title: 6.7 Computing with the Series
docs.text:
The series were used for computation, and their practical value is easily checked.

The sine of \(30^\circ\)

For \(\theta = 30^\circ = \pi/6 = 0.5235988\) radian, the successive terms of the sine series and their partial sums are:

Term Value Partial sum \(\theta\) \(0.5235988\) \(0.5235988\) \(-\theta^3/3!\) \(-0.0239246\) \(0.4996742\) \(+\theta^5/5!\) \(0.0003280\) \(0.5000021\) \(-\theta^7/7!\) \(-0.0000021\) \(0.5000000\)

Four terms give the sine of \(30^\circ\), which is exactly \(\tfrac12\), to seven decimal places.

\(\pi\) from ten terms

With ten terms of the series \(1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots - \tfrac{1}{19}\) the sum is \(0.7604599\), and \(4 \times 0.7604599 = 3.0418\), which is not even correct to one decimal place. Adding the third correction, \(F^{(3)}_{10} = \frac{101}{4000 + 50} = 0.0249383\), gives

\[4 \times (0.7604599 + 0.0249383) = 3.1415927,\]

correct to seven decimal places.

The faster series

The partial sums of \(\sqrt{12}\left(1 - \frac{1}{3\cdot 3} + \frac{1}{5\cdot 3^2} - \cdots\right)\) approach \(\pi\) quickly:

Terms Partial sum Terms Partial sum 1 3.4641016 10 3.1415905 2 3.0792014 15 3.141592660 3 3.1561815 21 3.14159265360 5 3.1426047

After 21 terms the error is less than \(10^{-11}\).

docs.title: 6.8 A Sine Table from the Series: Mādhava’s Constants
docs.text:
In principle the sine series gives the sine of any arc. In practice, an astronomer working in sexagesimal units, with arcs of several thousand minutes and a radius of 3438 minutes, faced large powers and long divisions at every term. A verse attributed to Mādhava, and quoted by Śaṅkara Vāriyar in his commentary on the Tantrasaṅgraha, removes most of this labour. It gives five numbers in the kaṭapayādi notation (Chapter 1) which, once memorised, turn the series into a short routine of multiplications and subtractions (Plofker 2009; Gold and Pingree 1991).

The idea is to measure every arc against the quadrant. Let the arc \(s\) be in minutes. The quadrant is \(q = 5400'\), and the radius is taken as \(R = 21600/2\pi = 3437'\,44”\,48”'\), the radius whose circumference is exactly \(21{,}600\) minutes. The sine series of Section 6.3 can then be written

\[R\sin\frac{s}{R} = s - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{3} c_3 + \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{5} c_5 - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{7} c_7 + \cdots, \qquad c_{2k+1} = \frac{q^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!\,R^{2k}} .\]

The numbers \(c_3, c_5, \ldots\) depend only on the quadrant and the radius, never on the arc, so they can be computed once and for all. Since \(s/q\) never exceeds 1, the remaining work involves only fractions of these fixed numbers. The terms can also be nested, so that each step needs one multiplication by \((s/q)^2\) and one subtraction:

\[R\sin\frac{s}{R} = s - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{3}\Biggl[c_3 - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{2}\biggl[c_5 - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{2}\Bigl[c_7 - \left(\frac{s}{q}\right)^{2}\bigl[c_9 - \left(\tfrac{s}{q}\right)^{2} c_{11}\bigr]\Bigr]\biggr]\Biggr].\]

This arrangement, which a modern reader would call Horner’s scheme, is the form in which the Kerala texts use the series. The verse is usually read as giving the five constants \(c_{11}, c_9, c_7, c_5, c_3\) in that order. Table 6.3 sets the recomputed values beside the number-words, which are given as they are usually cited; their grammatical endings do not affect the digits.

Table 6.3. The constants of the sine series, recomputed with \(q = 5400'\) and \(R = 21600/2\pi\), and the kaṭapayādi words that encode them Recomputed Rounded Word Digits as written \(c_{11}\) \(0'\,0”\,44.5”'\) \(45”'\) vidvān 4 4 \(c_{9}\) \(0'\,33”\,5.6”'\) \(33”\,6”'\) tunnabala 6 0 3 3 \(c_{7}\) \(16'\,5”\,40.9”'\) \(16'\,5”\,41”'\) kavīśanicaya 1 4 5 0 6 1 \(c_{5}\) \(273'\,57”\,47.0”'\) \(273'\,57”\,47”'\) sarvārthaśīlasthira 7 4 7 5 3 7 2 \(c_{3}\) \(2220'\,39”\,39.6”'\) \(2220'\,39”\,40”'\) nirviddhāṅganarendraruṅ 0 4 9 3 0 2 2 2

The words decode by the rules of Chapter 1. In kavīśanicaya, for instance, ka is 1, va 4, śa 5, na 0, ca 6 and ya 1. Read from the last syllable to the first, these give 160541, that is, \(16'\,05”\,41”'\). In the longer words, only the last consonant of each cluster counts (rva as va, rtha as tha, ddhā as dha, ndra as ra). A final consonant without a vowel, such as the ṅ at the end of nirviddhāṅganarendraruṅ, is not counted. Four of the decoded numbers agree with the recomputed constants to the nearest third of arc. The smallest, \(44”'\), lies half a third below the recomputed \(44.5”'\), a difference that alters no sine by more than half a third. The next constant, \(c_{13}\), would be only about \(0.7”'\), less than a third, which explains why the verse stops at five. A companion rule of the same kind is reported for the versed sine.

The sine of \(30^\circ\) with the five constants

For \(s = 1800'\) we have \(s/q = \tfrac13\), so each step multiplies by \(\tfrac19\), and the final factor is \((s/q)^3 = \tfrac{1}{27}\). Working to the nearest third:

Step Result \(c_9 - \tfrac19 c_{11} = 33”\,6”' - 4.9”'\) \(33”\,1”'\) \(c_7 - \tfrac19(33”\,1”')\) \(16'\,2”\,1”'\) \(c_5 - \tfrac19(16'\,2”\,1”')\) \(272'\,10”\,54”'\) \(c_3 - \tfrac19(272'\,10”\,54”')\) \(2190'\,25”\,7”'\) \(\tfrac{1}{27}(2190'\,25”\,7”')\) \(81'\,7”\,36”'\) \(1800' - 81'\,7”\,36”'\) \(1718'\,52”\,24”'\)

The sine of \(30^\circ\) is exactly half the radius, \(1718'\,52”\,24”'\) to the nearest third, and the routine reproduces it.

Applied to the other arcs of the table, with rounding only at the end, the same routine gives every one of the 24 sines within half a third of \(R\sin\theta\) (with \(R = 21600/2\pi\)): \(224'\,50”\,22”'\) for \(3^\circ 45'\), \(2430'\,51”\,15”'\) for \(45^\circ\), \(2977'\,10”\,34”'\) for \(60^\circ\), and, for the whole quadrant, the radius itself, \(3437'\,44”\,48”'\). This is the accuracy of the 24-sine table attributed to Mādhava, whose values are given to thirds (Section 6.3). The constants show that the series could produce such a table with a modest amount of arithmetic. The surviving texts do not record how Mādhava himself actually computed his table.

docs.title: 6.9 Astronomy and the Lunar Sentences
docs.text: The Kerala school was above all a school of astronomers, and its mathematics served the computation of planetary positions. In South India, positions of the Moon were commonly computed with the help of vākyas, “sentences” in the kaṭapayādi notation, each encoding the true longitude of the Moon on successive days of a cycle of about 248 days (nine anomalistic months). The standard set of such sentences was traditionally attributed to Vararuci. Mādhava’s Veṇvāroha gives a more accurate method, with sentences for shorter intervals and corrections derived from improved parameters. Parameśvara’s observations and Nīlakaṇṭha’s revisions of planetary theory belong to the same effort to bring computation into agreement with the sky (Plofker 2009; Sarma 1972).

docs.title: 6.10.1 Parameśvara
docs.text:
Parameśvara of Vaṭaśśeri (c. 1360–1455), a pupil of Mādhava, is known above all for his observations. He reports eclipse observations over more than fifty years and, finding that the computed positions no longer agreed with the sky, prepared a revised system, the Dṛggaṇita (“calculation [agreeing with] observation”), in 1431. In mathematics he gave a formula for the radius of the circle circumscribing a cyclic quadrilateral with sides \(a, b, c, d\), studied by R. C. Gupta (Gupta 1977):

\[R = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{\frac{(ab+cd)(ac+bd)(ad+bc)}{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}},\]

where \(s\) is the semiperimeter. For the quadrilateral 25, 39, 60, 52 of Chapter 4 it gives \(R = 32.5\), half the diameter 65. He also used iterative methods for solving astronomical equations that cannot be solved directly.

docs.title: 6.10.2 Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī
docs.text:
Nīlakaṇṭha (1444–c. 1545), of Trikkaṇṭiyūr near Tirur, was a Nambūtiri Brahmin who had performed the Vedic Soma sacrifice, hence his title Somayājī. His Tantrasaṅgraha (1500) is an astronomical treatise, and his long commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya discusses many mathematical questions. He explains that the ratio of circumference to diameter cannot be expressed exactly as a ratio of whole numbers, and he quotes the series attributed to Mādhava.

Commenting on Āryabhaṭa’s word āsanna (“approximate”) in the verse on the circumference (Chapter 3), Nīlakaṇṭha asks why Āryabhaṭa gave an approximate value instead of the exact one. His answer is that the exact value cannot be given: if the diameter is measured by some unit, the circumference measured by the same unit will always leave a remainder, however small the unit is made, and so the two can never both be expressed in whole numbers. This is a clear statement that the circumference and the diameter are incommensurable—that \(\pi\) is not a ratio of integers. Nīlakaṇṭha gives it as a reasoned assertion, not as a proof in the modern sense; a proof that \(\pi\) is irrational was first given by J. H. Lambert in 1761 (Lambert 1768).

In the Tantrasaṅgraha and later works, Nīlakaṇṭha revised the traditional planetary models. In his scheme the five planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn move around the mean Sun, which itself moves around the earth. K. Ramasubramanian, M. D. Srinivas and M. S. Sriram pointed out in 1994 that this geometrical arrangement resembles the system later proposed by Tycho Brahe (1588). The resemblance is real and interesting, but the models were reached independently and for different reasons, and Nīlakaṇṭha’s computational scheme remained geocentric (Ramasubramanian et al. 1994; Ramasubramanian and Sriram 2011).

docs.title: 6.10.3 Citrabhānu, Śaṅkara Vāriyar and Acyuta
docs.text:
Citrabhānu (fl. 1530) wrote a short work, the Ekaviṃśatipraśnottara (“Answers to twenty-one questions”), on finding two unknown numbers when any two of seven quantities are given: their sum, difference, product, the sum and difference of their squares, and the sum and difference of their cubes. There are \(\binom{7}{2} = 21\) such pairs of data, and he solves each case, giving algebraic justifications.

Śaṅkara Vāriyar (c. 1500–1560), a member of the Vāriyar community of temple servants and a pupil of Nīlakaṇṭha, wrote two great commentaries: the Kriyākramakarī on the Līlāvatī, completed after his death by Mahiṣamaṅgalam Nārāyaṇa, and the Yuktidīpikā on the Tantrasaṅgraha. Both contain Sanskrit versions of the derivations found in the Yuktibhāṣā, and they preserve verses attributed to Mādhava.

Acyuta Piṣāraṭi (c. 1550–1621), a pupil of Jyeṣṭhadeva, wrote on the computation of true planetary positions and on the reduction of positions to the ecliptic, and he taught the poet and grammarian Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri.

docs.title: 6.10.4 Later works
docs.text: The Karaṇapaddhati, attributed to Putumana Somayājī and variously dated between the late sixteenth and the early eighteenth century, is a manual of astronomical computation that makes extensive use of the series. It also lists a sequence of increasingly accurate fractional approximations to \(\pi\), among them \(355/113\), a value also known in China in the fifth century (Zu Chongzhi). The Sadratnamālā of Śaṅkara Varman (1819 or 1823; sources differ), a Kerala prince, restated the series and gave \(\pi\) to seventeen decimal places; it was one of the sources used by Whish (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 6.11 Social Setting
docs.text: The Kerala school worked within the Brahmin and temple-servant communities of central Kerala. Nīlakaṇṭha, Parameśvara and Jyeṣṭhadeva were Nambūtiri Brahmins; Śaṅkara Vāriyar and Acyuta Piṣāraṭi belonged to the ambalavāsi communities attached to temples. Teaching took place in the households (illam) of scholarly families and was supported by landholdings, by temples and by local rulers. The school’s knowledge was thus confined to a small group, and it depended on the continuity of a few teaching lineages; when these weakened in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the mathematical tradition faded, although astronomical practice using its results continued. The use of Malayalam in the Yuktibhāṣā, unusual for a technical work, suggests an audience that was at home in the regional language as well as in Sanskrit (Sarma 1972; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.12 Rediscovery
docs.text: The Kerala series were first reported in Europe by Charles M. Whish, an official of the East India Company, in a paper read in 1832 and published in 1834 in the Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society. Whish described the series in the Tantrasaṅgraha, the Yuktibhāṣā, the Karaṇapaddhati and the Sadratnamālā (Whish 1834). His paper attracted little attention. From the 1940s C. T. Rajagopal and his collaborators, notably M. S. Rangachari, published studies showing the mathematical content of the derivations, and K. V. Sarma edited the principal texts and wrote a history of the school (1972) (Rajagopal and Rangachari 1978; Sarma 1972). Since then the subject has become part of the general history of mathematics, and Kim Plofker’s survey of 2009 gives it a central place (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.13 The Question of Transmission to Europe
docs.text:
Could the Kerala series have reached Europe and influenced Gregory, Newton or Leibniz? Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries were active on the Kerala coast from the early sixteenth century; the Jesuits ran colleges, took an interest in Indian astronomy and calendars, and corresponded with Rome, where Christoph Clavius led the reform of the calendar. On this basis George Gheverghese Joseph, C. K. Raju and others have argued that Kerala mathematics may have been carried to Europe (Joseph 2011; Raju 2007).

No document has been found that records such a transmission: no translation of a Kerala text, no letter describing the series, no European manuscript that uses them. The European development of infinite series in the seventeenth century can be followed step by step in the surviving works of Cavalieri, Wallis, Mercator, Gregory, Newton and Leibniz, and it grew out of problems in the geometry of curves and the binomial theorem rather than from trigonometric tables. Most historians, including Kim Plofker, therefore regard the European results as independent, while accepting that transmission cannot be ruled out entirely. The question remains open, but the burden of evidence lies on those who assert transmission, and this volume does not assert it (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.14 Assessment
docs.text: The Kerala school found the power series for the sine, cosine and arctangent and the series for \(\pi\), invented corrections that turned a slowly converging series into a practical method of computation, computed \(\pi\) to eleven places, and explained these results in reasoned derivations based on the summation of indefinitely many small quantities. It reached them by its own path, through trigonometry, astronomy and the long Indian tradition of finite differences and series, and it wrote the reasoning down, in Malayalam prose as well as Sanskrit verse, with a care for stated approximations that is rare in any premodern tradition. Whether the result should be called calculus is, as Section 6.6 shows, a question of definition on which careful scholars disagree. The school’s weakness was social rather than mathematical. Confined to a few families and supported by local patrons, its work was not taken up outside Kerala, and within two centuries the mathematics was remembered mainly through the astronomical rules that used it (Plofker 2009; Divakaran 2018; Sarma 1972).

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Sum the first five terms of the series \(1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \cdots\) and apply the third Kerala correction. How accurate is the resulting value of \(\pi\)?

  2. Use four terms of the sine series to compute \(\sin 1\) (one radian).

  3. Check that Mādhava’s value \(2{,}827{,}433{,}388{,}233/(9\times 10^{11})\) agrees with \(\pi\) to eleven decimal places.

  4. Compute \(S_2(50) = 1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + 50^2\) and compare it with \(50^3/3\).

  5. Verify that \(F(n) = \frac{1}{4n}\) satisfies \(F(n) + F(n+1) - \frac{1}{2n+1} = \frac{1}{4n(n+1)(2n+1)}\).

  6. Use Parameśvara’s formula to find the circumradius of the cyclic quadrilateral with sides 36, 77, 75, 40.

Answers. (1) \(4\left(0.834921 - \frac{26}{525}\right) = 3.1415873\), with an error of about \(5 \times 10^{-6}\). (2) \(1 - \frac16 + \frac{1}{120} - \frac{1}{5040} = 0.841468\); true \(0.841471\). (3) \(3.14159265359\ldots\) against \(3.14159265358979\ldots\) (4) \(42{,}925\) against \(41{,}666.7\): about 3% too large. (5) \(\frac{1}{4n} + \frac{1}{4(n+1)} = \frac{2n+1}{4n(n+1)}\), and \(\frac{2n+1}{4n(n+1)} - \frac{1}{2n+1} = \frac{(2n+1)^2 - 4n(n+1)}{4n(n+1)(2n+1)} = \frac{1}{4n(n+1)(2n+1)}\). (6) \(42\frac12\), half the diameter 85.

Scholarly Note: Further reading

The edition and translation of the Yuktibhāṣā by Sarma, Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram (2008) is the essential source; Ramasubramanian and Sriram (2011) translate the Tantrasaṅgraha. Sarma (1972) gives a history of the school; Plofker (2009), chapter 7, and Divakaran (2018) discuss the mathematics; Hayashi, Kusuba and Yano (1990) analyse the corrections; Roy (1990) compares the Kerala and European derivations of the series for \(\pi\). On the “calculus” question, Divakaran (2007) and Ramasubramanian and Srinivas (2010) argue the strong case, and Katz (1995) the cautious one (Sarma et al. 2008; Ramasubramanian and Sriram 2011; Sarma 1972; Divakaran 2018, 2007; Hayashi et al. 1990; Roy 1990; Ramasubramanian and Srinivas 2010; Katz 1995).

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Decimal Place-Value System and Zero
docs.text: The numerals used throughout the world today—ten digits whose value depends on their position, with a sign for an empty place—were first developed in India. They reached the Islamic world by the eighth century and Europe from the tenth, and by the sixteenth century they had displaced the Roman numerals and the abacus in European commerce and science. They are usually called “Hindu–Arabic” numerals, a name that records both their origin and the route by which they travelled. This chapter examines the evidence for their development in India, the separate history of zero as a number, and their transmission (Plofker 2009; Hayashi 2003; Ifrah 2000; Menninger 1969).

docs.title: 7.1 Three Meanings of “Zero”
docs.text:
The history of zero is often confused because the word covers three different things:

  1. A placeholder: a way of showing, in a positional notation, that a place is empty, as in \(305\), where the tens place is empty.

  2. A written sign for that empty place, such as a dot or a small circle.

  3. A number: a quantity that can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided according to rules, and that can be the result of a calculation, as in \(5 - 5 = 0\).

The first two had been developed in other cultures. Babylonian astronomers of the Seleucid period (from about 300 BCE) used a sign to mark an empty place in their sexagesimal (base-60) numbers, though not at the end of a number; Greek astronomers, including Ptolemy, used a symbol for an empty place in sexagesimal fractions; and the Maya of Mesoamerica had a zero sign in their positional calendrical numbers. What is distinctive in India is the combination of a decimal place-value system, a sign for zero used in every position, and—from Brahmagupta onward—rules for operating with zero as a number.

docs.title: 7.2 Numerals Before Place Value
docs.text: The earliest Indian numerals, found in Brāhmī inscriptions from the third century BCE onward, were not positional. In the Nānāghāṭ cave inscription (1st century BCE) and later Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī inscriptions, there are separate signs for 1 to 9, for each multiple of ten from 10 to 90, for 100 and 1000, and combinations for multiples of these. To write 345 one wrote the sign for 300, then the sign for 40, then the sign for 5. Such a system, like the Greek alphabetic numerals, needs no zero. Some of the forms of the units 4 to 9 in these inscriptions are recognisable ancestors of the later place-value digits (Ifrah 2000; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 7.3.1 Word-numerals
docs.text:
The first evidence for decimal place value in India comes not from written digits but from words. In the word-numeral (bhūtasaṃkhyā) system described in Chapter 1, digits are represented by words and listed from the units upward, and a word for “empty” (śūnya, kha, ambara) is used for an empty place. Wherever such word-numerals appear with a word for zero, place value is implied.

  • The Yavanajātaka of Sphujidhvaja, a Sanskrit verse adaptation of a Greek astrological work, uses word-numerals including śūnya. David Pingree dated it to 269/270 CE on the basis of a verse that he read as giving the date. In 2013, Bill Mak, using a newly identified manuscript, argued that the verse had been misread and that the text cannot be dated so precisely. The Yavanajātaka therefore no longer provides a secure third-century date for zero (Mak 2013).

  • The Lokavibhāga, a Digambara Jain cosmological text, states that it was copied in Śaka 380 (458 CE) and uses word-numerals with śūnya in a place-value way. The surviving Sanskrit text is a later version of an earlier Prakrit work, and how much of it goes back to 458 is debated.

  • Āryabhaṭa (499) names the decimal places, extracts square and cube roots by place-value methods, and designs his alphabetic notation on a decimal basis (Chapter 3).

  • Varāhamihira’s Pañcasiddhāntikā (mid-6th century) and the astronomers after him use word-numerals with zero routinely.

By the sixth century, then, the decimal place-value system with a concept of zero was in standard use among Indian astronomers.

docs.title: 7.3.2 The Bakhshālī manuscript
