Like the astronomical texts, the arithmetic books state their rules in verse, usually in the āryā or anuṣṭubh metres, so that they could be memorised. A rule (sūtra or karaṇasūtra) is followed by one or more examples (udāharaṇa), also in verse. The examples are not decorative: they fix the meaning of a compressed rule by showing which quantity is which. A commentary, written by the author himself or by a later teacher, then sets down the data of each example (nyāsa), works through the computation and, often, checks the result. Much of what we know about the actual practice of calculation comes from these commentaries and from the solved examples of the Bakhshālī manuscript (Section 10.2) (Plofker 2009; Keller 2006).

The examples give the books much of their charm. They are set among merchants, travellers, kings and lovers, in gardens and temples, and the poets among the mathematicians—Mahāvīra and Bhāskara II above all—wrote them with literary care. They also give the historian a picture, partial and stylised, of the economic life the books served: the units of money and weight, the goods traded, the rates of interest, the wages of labourers and the prices of animals and of slaves.

docs.title: 10.1.3 Readers and purposes
docs.text:
The arithmetic books were written for several kinds of reader at once. Students of astronomy needed fluent calculation before they could approach the siddhāntas. Merchants, moneylenders, goldsmiths and officials needed proportion, interest and the reduction of mixed units. Builders and surveyors needed areas and volumes. The authors addressed all of these. Mahāvīra opens his book with a list of the activities in which calculation is required—worldly, Vedic and religious affairs, love and economics, music and drama, cookery and medicine, architecture and prosody, logic and grammar—in the passage that ends with the verse quoted at the head of Chapter 1 (Rangācārya 1912). Such statements are partly rhetorical, but the range of examples in the books bears them out.

The arithmetic books were also the first Indian mathematical texts that were not chapters of astronomical works. Their authors were not always astronomers: Mahāvīra’s surviving work is purely mathematical, and the later vernacular arithmetics (Chapter 13) were written by officials and poets. The genre thus shows mathematics becoming a subject of its own, taught and used outside the circle of the jyotiṣa families.

docs.title: 10.2 The Bakhshālī Manuscript as a Book of Problems
docs.text: Chapter 2 (Section 2.4) described the discovery of the Bakhshālī manuscript, its notation, its rule for approximate square roots and the controversy over its date. Here it is considered as an example of what an arithmetic book looked like in use, since it is the only one to survive in an early physical copy with its worked solutions.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Form and layout
docs.text: The manuscript contains rules, examples and solutions in a fixed order. A rule in verse is followed by an example; the data of the example are then written out in a table ruled into compartments, each holding a number or a fraction, with abbreviations marking the role of each entry; the computation follows, and the answer is often verified by substituting it back into the conditions of the problem. Fractions are written in vertical columns, and negative quantities are marked by a sign after the number (Chapter 2). The language is a non-standard Sanskrit with many Prakrit features, the kind of Sanskrit used by people who wrote it for practical purposes rather than as literature. G. R. Kaye’s edition (1927–33) published photographs of the leaves; Takao Hayashi’s edition (1995) reconstructed the order of the surviving material, much of which is damaged or out of sequence, and identified the rules and examples (Kaye 1927; Hayashi 1995).

docs.title: 10.2.2 Problem types
docs.text:
The surviving problems cover much of the later arithmetic syllabus: linear equations in one and several unknowns, often of the “equal wealth” type; arithmetic progressions, including problems about travellers whose daily journeys increase in progression; problems of profit and loss and of purchase and sale; the rule of three; and quadratic problems leading to the extraction of square roots, where the square-root rule of Chapter 2 is put to work. Many problems are solved by the method of “false position” (supposition): a convenient value is assumed for the unknown, the conditions of the problem are applied to it, and the assumed value is corrected in proportion to the error. The method appears in the later Sanskrit books as iṣṭakarman, “operation with an assumed number”, and it was also standard in Egyptian, Chinese, Islamic and medieval European arithmetic (Hayashi 1995; Datta and Singh 1935).

Worked example: false position

A problem often cited from the manuscript runs: a merchant pays duty at three places; at the first he gives a third of his goods, at the second a quarter of what remains, at the third a fifth of what then remains; the total duty is 24. How much did he have at first? (Joseph 2011) Solution by false position. Assume 60, which is divisible by 3, 4 and 5. The duties are then \(20\), \(\tfrac14 \times 40 = 10\) and \(\tfrac15 \times 30 = 6\), a total of 36, and 24 remains. The true duty is 24, not 36, so the true amount is \(60 \times \tfrac{24}{36} = 40\). Check. From 40 the duties are \(13\tfrac13\), \(6\tfrac23\) and 4, which add up to 24; \(16\) remains.

The method works because the answer is proportional to the data: whatever the original amount, the duty is a fixed fraction of it, here \(1 - \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac45 = \tfrac35\). The same reasoning solves a second type of problem, in which several people’s gifts or contributions stand in given ratios. If A gives an amount, B twice as much, C three times as much as B and D four times as much as C, and the gifts total 132, then assuming that A gives 1 makes the total \(1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33\); the true value of A’s gift is therefore \(132/33 = 4\).

Worked example: a traveller in progression

One traveller goes 18 yojanas each day. A second starts at the same time and place, going 3 yojanas on the first day, 6 on the second, 9 on the third, and so on. When does the second overtake the first? After \(n\) days the first has gone \(18n\) and the second \(3 + 6 + \cdots + 3n = \tfrac32 n(n+1)\). They are level when \(\tfrac32 n(n+1) = 18n\), that is, when \(n + 1 = 12\): after 11 days, when both have gone 198 yojanas.

The numbers here are chosen for illustration. The manuscript’s problems of this type lead in general to quadratic equations, solved by the rule for the number of terms of a progression (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 10.2.3 Verification
docs.text:
The habit of verification is the manuscript’s most striking feature. After a solution the scribe often writes the word for “check” (pratyaya) and recomputes the conditions of the problem from the answer, showing that they are satisfied. For approximate square roots, the check consists in squaring the approximation and comparing it with the original number, with the small excess noted. This practice—computing, then confirming by reversing the computation—is found throughout later Indian arithmetic, and it is one source of the tradition’s justifications of its rules (Chapter 1).

The dispute over the date (Section 2.4) does not affect this content, only its place in history. On Hayashi’s dating the work stands at the head of the tradition of arithmetic books, beside Bhāskara I’s commentary, and that is how it is read here.

docs.title: 10.3 Śrīdhara: The Pāṭīgaṇita and the Triśatikā
10.3.1 The author and his works
docs.text: Śrīdhara is known only from his works and from references to them by later authors; his date, usually put around 750 CE, rests on his relation to Brahmagupta and to Mahāvīra, and dates as late as the tenth century have been proposed. The opening invocation of the Pāṭīgaṇita is addressed to Śiva, and K. S. Shukla, who edited it, took him to be a Śaiva; the claim that he was a Jain rests on weaker grounds. Two arithmetic works survive. The Pāṭīgaṇita is the larger; it survives in a single incomplete manuscript, with an anonymous commentary, and breaks off before the end of the determinations. The Pāṭīgaṇitasāra (“Essence of the Pāṭīgaṇita”), known as the Triśatikā because it has about three hundred verses, is an abridgement that covers the whole syllabus and was widely copied and commented on. A work on algebra is lost, but later authors quote from it, and Bhāskara II gives Śrīdhara’s rule for the quadratic equation (Chapter 5). Śrīdhara also states rules for zero: adding zero to a number or subtracting it leaves the number unchanged, and multiplying by zero gives zero (Shukla 1959; Plofker 2009; Datta and Singh 1935).

docs.title: 10.3.2 Fractions and their classes
docs.text:
Śrīdhara treats fractions systematically. After the operations on simple fractions he classifies the compound expressions met in practice into types (jāti), each with its own rule of reduction to a single fraction. The most common are:

  • bhāga: fractions to be added or subtracted, such as \(\tfrac12 + \tfrac13\);

  • prabhāga: a fraction of a fraction, such as \(\tfrac12\) of \(\tfrac34\);

  • bhāgabhāga: a quantity divided by a fraction, such as \(1 \div \tfrac34\);

  • bhāgānubandha: a fraction “increased by” a fraction of itself, such as a quarter increased by its own third;

  • bhāgāpavāha: a fraction “diminished by” a fraction of itself, such as a half diminished by its own fifth.

Mahāvīra adopts the same classes and adds a sixth, bhāgamātṛ, for expressions that combine several of the others. The classification reflects the way such quantities were spoken of in trade—“a quarter and a third of it”, “half less a fifth”—and the rules translate everyday phrases into exact arithmetic (Shukla 1959; Datta and Singh 1935).

Worked example: the classes of fractions

Association (bhāgānubandha). A quarter increased by its own third is \(\tfrac14 + \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac14\left(1 + \tfrac13\right) = \tfrac13\). Dissociation (bhāgāpavāha). A half diminished by its own fifth is \(\tfrac12\left(1 - \tfrac15\right) = \tfrac25\). Fraction of a fraction (prabhāga). Two-thirds of three-quarters of five-sixths of 72 is \(72 \times \tfrac56 \times \tfrac34 \times \tfrac23 = 30\). The rules are written so that the result is reached by multiplying numerators and denominators in a fixed order; the commentaries then reduce the result to lowest terms.

docs.title: 10.3.3 Proportion and the determinations
docs.text: Śrīdhara’s statement of the rule of three, with its three terms—the “measure” (pramāṇa), its “fruit” (phala) and the “requisition” (icchā)—and his rules for the inverse rule and for proportions with five, seven, nine and eleven terms became the model for later books; they are described in Chapter 11. His determinations follow Brahmagupta’s eight: mixtures (including interest and the purchase and sale of goods), series, plane figures, excavations, piles, sawing, heaps of grain and shadows. In each he gives both “gross” and more accurate rules where the tradition had them, and in each the examples are drawn from practical life (Shukla 1959).

docs.title: 10.3.4 The volume of the sphere
docs.text:
One of Śrīdhara’s mensuration rules shows how the arithmetic books improved inherited results. Āryabhaṭa’s rule for the volume of a sphere—the area of a great circle multiplied by its own square root—is wrong (Chapter 3). Śrīdhara instead takes half the cube of the diameter and adds to it its own eighteenth part, that is \(V = \tfrac{19}{36}\,d^3\). Mahāvīra gives a “gross” value of \(\tfrac92 r^3\) and an “accurate” value nine-tenths of this. Bhāskara II, finally, gives the exact rule, the surface multiplied by the diameter and divided by six (Chapter 5). Table 10.1 compares them.

Table 10.1. Rules for the volume of a sphere of radius \(r\), as multiples of \(r^3\) Author Rule (modern form) Coefficient Error Āryabhaṭa (499) \(\pi r^2 \sqrt{\pi r^2}\) 5.568 \(+32.9\%\) Śrīdhara (c. 750?) \(\tfrac{19}{36}d^3 = \tfrac{38}{9}r^3\) 4.222 \(+0.8\%\) Mahāvīra, gross (c. 850) \(\tfrac92 r^3\) 4.500 \(+7.4\%\) Mahāvīra, accurate \(\tfrac{9}{10}\cdot\tfrac92 r^3\) 4.050 \(-3.3\%\) Bhāskara II (1150) \(\tfrac{1}{6} S d = \tfrac43 \pi r^3\) 4.189 exact

Śrīdhara’s coefficient is the best of the approximate rules; it corresponds to a value of \(\pi\) of \(\tfrac{19}{6} \approx 3.17\) in the exact formula \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}d^3\). How he arrived at it is not known.

docs.title: 10.4 Mahāvīra’s Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha
docs.text: Mahāvīra, a Jain, wrote the Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha (“Compendium of the essence of calculation”) around 850 at Mānyakheṭa in Karnataka, at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I (r. 814–878), whom he praises at the beginning of the work. With more than a thousand verses of rules and examples it is the largest and most systematic of the early arithmetic books. Its nine chapters treat terminology (saṃjñā), the operations (parikarma), fractions (kalāsavarṇa), miscellaneous problems (prakīrṇaka), the rule of three (trairāśika), mixed problems (miśraka), plane figures (kṣetra), excavations (khāta) and shadows (chāyā). M. Rangācārya edited and translated it in 1912. This section follows the book through, chapter by chapter, to show the range and the method of a ninth-century arithmetic (Rangācārya 1912; Plofker 2009; Datta and Singh 1935).

docs.title: 10.4.1 Terminology and the scale of numbers
docs.text: The first chapter (saṃjñā) defines the units of length, area, volume, time, grain, gold, silver and other metals that the problems use, and the rules for positive and negative quantities and zero. A negative number, Mahāvīra says, has no square root, “since it is not a square by nature”; and a number divided by zero remains unchanged, a rule that later authors did not follow (Table 7.2). The chapter also names the decimal places. Mahāvīra’s list runs to twenty-four places, from eka (units) through daśa (tens), śata (hundreds) and sahasra (thousands) to mahākṣobha, the place of \(10^{23}\); such lists, which differ from author to author in their higher names, show how naturally the place-value system was extended to very large numbers.

docs.title: 10.4.2 The eight operations
docs.text:
The second chapter (parikarman) treats eight operations: multiplication, division, squaring, square root, cubing, cube root, the summation of series (saṅkalita) and the subtraction of a part of a series from the whole (vyutkalita). Addition and subtraction are not counted separately; they are taken for granted. Square and cube roots are extracted digit by digit, the digits of the number being marked off alternately as “odd” (viṣama) and “even” (sama) places for square roots, and in groups of three for cube roots, as in the method still taught in schools.

Among the multiplication exercises (2.10–17) are products whose results read like strings of beads, which Mahāvīra calls “necklaces”. Those he names so include

\[12345679 \times 9 = 111111111,\quad 14287143 \times 7 = 100010001,\quad 152207 \times 73 = 11111111,\]

and other exercises, such as \(139 \times 109 = 15151\), give similar patterns without the name. Such exercises gave practice in long multiplication and, at the same time, a check: an error anywhere spoils the pattern (Rangācārya 1912; Joseph 2011).

Worked example: summation and “subtraction” of series

Summation (saṅkalita). A progression with first term 4, common difference 3 and 10 terms has the sum \(\tfrac{10}{2}\left[2\cdot 4 + 9 \cdot 3\right] = 5 \times 35 = 175\). Subtraction (vyutkalita). The sum of the last six terms of the same progression is the whole sum less the sum of the first four: the first four terms sum to \(\tfrac42[8 + 9] = 34\), so the last six sum to \(175 - 34 = 141\). Directly: \(16 + 19 + 22 + 25 + 28 + 31 = 141\). Mahāvīra’s rules for vyutkalita let one find the sum of any run of terms in the middle of a progression without writing the terms out. Geometric progression. The sum of \(n\) terms with first term \(a\) and ratio \(r\) is \(a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1)\). With \(a = 3\), \(r = 5\), \(n = 4\): \(3 \cdot \frac{625 - 1}{4} = 468\), and indeed \(3 + 15 + 75 + 375 = 468\).

docs.title: 10.4.3 Fractions
docs.text:
The third chapter (kalāsavarṇa, “reduction of fractions”) covers the six classes of compound fractions described above and an unusually full treatment of unit fractions—fractions with numerator one. One rule writes 1 as a sum of any chosen number \(n \ge 3\) of unit fractions,

\[1 = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{3^{n-2}}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 3^{n-2}},\]

so that with five terms \(1 = \frac12 + \frac13 + \frac19 + \frac1{27} + \frac1{54}\), since \(27 + 18 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 54\); another splits a unit fraction into two, \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{q+1} + \frac{1}{q(q+1)}\), as in \(\frac13 = \frac14 + \frac1{12}\). He gives further rules for writing a given fraction as a sum of unit fractions, for writing 1 as a sum of fractions whose numerators are given, and for related problems. Takanori Kusuba has analysed these rules and shown how they fit together. One of them splits a fraction into a unit fraction and a remainder, choosing an auxiliary number so that the division comes out exactly; applied repeatedly with the smallest such number, it gives the procedure later described in Europe by Fibonacci (Kusuba 2004; Rangācārya 1912).

Worked example: splitting a fraction into unit fractions

To write \(\tfrac27\) as a sum of unit fractions, take the largest unit fraction not larger than it: since \(7/2 = 3\tfrac12\), this is \(\tfrac14\). The remainder is \(\tfrac27 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac{8 - 7}{28} = \tfrac{1}{28}\), already a unit fraction. So \(\tfrac27 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac{1}{28}\). For \(\tfrac{3}{7}\): the first unit fraction is \(\tfrac13\), and \(\tfrac37 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac{2}{21}\); for \(\tfrac{2}{21}\) the next is \(\tfrac{1}{11}\), and \(\tfrac{2}{21} - \tfrac{1}{11} = \tfrac{1}{231}\). So \(\tfrac37 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac1{11} + \tfrac1{231}\).

Why so much attention to unit fractions? The units of money and measure were divided into halves, quarters, sixteenths and other simple parts, and a fraction expressed as a sum of such parts could be paid or measured out directly. The interest may also have been partly recreational: the problems are ingenious, and some have no practical use at all.

docs.title: 10.4.4 Miscellaneous problems
docs.text:
The fourth chapter (prakīrṇaka) collects problems in which an unknown whole—a herd, a swarm, a sum of money—is to be found from statements about its parts. Mahāvīra sorts them into named types according to the form of the conditions: in the “fraction” type (bhāga) given fractions of the whole are removed and a known remainder is left; in the “remainder” type (śeṣa) the fractions are taken successively from what remains; in the “root” type (mūla) a multiple of the square root of the whole is removed as well; and there are further types combining these. Each type has its own rule. The “root” types lead to quadratic equations, and the rule for them is in effect the solution of a quadratic in the square root of the unknown.

Worked example: a problem of the “root” type

Of a flock of peacocks, a quarter and twice the square root of the whole flock went to the hills, and 32 remained. How many peacocks were there? (Numbers chosen for illustration.) Let the flock be \(x = y^2\). Then \(y^2 - \tfrac14 y^2 - 2y = 32\), that is \(\tfrac34 y^2 - 2y - 32 = 0\). The rule for this type amounts to

\[y = \frac{\tfrac{c}{2} + \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{c}{2}\right)^2 + (1-a)\,r}}{1 - a},\]

where \(a = \tfrac14\) is the fraction removed, \(c = 2\) the multiplier of the root and \(r = 32\) the remainder:

\[y = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 24}}{3/4} = \frac{6}{3/4} = 8 .\]

The flock had \(x = 64\) peacocks. Check. \(\tfrac14 \cdot 64 = 16\) and \(2\sqrt{64} = 16\) went away, and \(64 - 32 = 32\) remained.

The Līlāvatī’s problem of the bees (Chapter 5) belongs to the simplest, “fraction” type; Bhāskara II also has problems of the root type, which he solves by the same rule.

docs.title: 10.4.5 Proportion and mixtures
docs.text:
The fifth chapter treats the rule of three, direct and inverse, and the sixth, “mixed problems” (miśraka), is the longest in the book. It contains problems of interest, of the division of profits, of purchase and sale, a long section on mixtures of gold of different fineness, the rule for combinations illustrated with the six tastes (Chapter 8), and a section of “curious” problems solved with the pulveriser (vicitrakuṭṭīkāra). The commercial material is discussed in Chapter 11. The pulveriser problems include the type in which a given sum of money buys a given number of animals or birds of several kinds at different prices. This type is also well known in China: the Zhang Qiujian suanjing (fifth century) asks how 100 coins can buy 100 fowls, when a cock costs 5 coins, a hen 3, and three chicks cost 1.

Worked example: the “hundred fowls” type

With the Chinese numbers: if \(c\) cocks, \(h\) hens and \(k\) chicks are bought, then \(c + h + k = 100\) and \(5c + 3h + \tfrac13 k = 100\). Multiplying the second equation by 3 and subtracting the first gives \(14c + 8h = 200\), or \(7c + 4h = 100\). This is a linear indeterminate equation of the kind solved by the pulveriser. Its solutions in non-negative whole numbers are \(c = 0, 4, 8, 12\) with \(h = 25, 18, 11, 4\), and then \(k = 75, 78, 81, 84\). Check for \(c = 4\): \(4 + 18 + 78 = 100\) birds and \(20 + 54 + 26 = 100\) coins.

docs.title: 10.4.6 Plane figures, excavations and shadows
docs.text:
The seventh chapter (kṣetra) gives “practical” (vyāvahārika) and “accurate” (sūkṣma) rules for triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, segments of circles and a number of composite figures, among them the ring, the figure shaped like a drum and the “elongated circle” (āyatavṛtta). It also treats “generated” (janya) figures, triangles and quadrilaterals whose sides and areas are rational, constructed from rational right triangles in the manner of Brahmagupta (Chapter 4). For the elongated circle, an oval with length \(L\) and breadth \(B\), Mahāvīra’s more accurate rule for the perimeter is equivalent to

\[P \approx \sqrt{6B^2 + 4L^2}.\]

For a circle (\(L = B = d\)) it reduces to \(\sqrt{10}\,d\), the Jain value of the circumference (Chapter 2).

Worked example: the perimeter of an oval

Take an oval of length \(L = 10\) and breadth \(B = 6\). Mahāvīra’s rule gives \(P \approx \sqrt{6\cdot 36 + 4 \cdot 100} = \sqrt{616} \approx 24.82\). If the figure is an ellipse with these axes, its true perimeter is \(25.53\) (to two decimal places), so the rule is about \(2.8\%\) too small. No simple exact formula for the perimeter of an ellipse exists; it requires an elliptic integral. One of the best simple approximations was published by Ramanujan in 1914 (Chapter 14): with semi-axes \(a = 5\), \(b = 3\), his formula \(\pi\left[3(a+b) - \sqrt{(3a+b)(a+3b)}\right]\) gives \(25.5270\), agreeing with the true value to four decimal places. The comparison is between two very different aims: Mahāvīra wanted a rule that a surveyor could apply, and it is not known whether he meant his oval to be an ellipse at all.

The eighth chapter (khāta) treats the volumes of excavations, including pits whose top and bottom differ, of spheres (Table 10.1) and of piles of bricks; the ninth (chāyā) treats shadows. Their rules are discussed with the other rules for builders in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 10.4.7 Reception
docs.text: The Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha was copied and studied above all in the South, and it is from South Indian manuscripts that M. Rangācārya edited it in 1912. It was adapted into Telugu by Pāvulūri Mallana and was known to the Kannada mathematical writers (Chapter 13). In the North its place was taken, from the twelfth century, by the Līlāvatī. Mahāvīra’s book is also the main witness to the mathematical culture of the Jain community, but its methods are those of the general tradition, and its problems, though often framed with Jain imagery, are addressed to any reader who calculates (Rangācārya 1912; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 10.5 Finding Unknowns Without Algebra
docs.text: The arithmetic books solve many problems that we would solve with an equation, but they do so without writing down an unknown. Instead they teach a handful of general methods, each suited to a particular shape of problem. Four of them recur in every book from Āryabhaṭa to Nārāyaṇa: inversion, supposition, concurrence and the “dissimilar operation”. Together they cover most of the problems in one unknown that arise in practice, and they show how far a purely arithmetical approach could go.

docs.title: 10.5.1 Inversion
docs.text:
When a number has been subjected to a known chain of operations and the final result is given, the original number is found by “inversion” (viloma or vyastavidhi): one starts from the result and undoes the operations in reverse order, dividing where the problem multiplied, subtracting where it added, taking the square root where it squared, and so on. Āryabhaṭa states the method in a single verse of the Gaṇitapāda (Chapter 3). The only subtle point concerns fractional increases. If a number was increased by \(\tfrac{a}{b}\) of itself, it was multiplied by \(\tfrac{a+b}{b}\), and to undo this it must be diminished by \(\tfrac{a}{a+b}\) of itself; Bhāskara II gives exactly this rule, and the corresponding one for a fractional decrease.

Worked example: inversion in the Līlāvatī

Bhāskara II asks for the number which, multiplied by 3, increased by three-quarters of the product, divided by 7, diminished by a third of the quotient, multiplied by itself, diminished by 52, square-rooted, increased by 8 and divided by 10, gives 2 (Colebrooke 1817). Inversion. Start from 2 and reverse each step: \(2 \times 10 = 20\); \(20 - 8 = 12\); \(12^2 = 144\); \(144 + 52 = 196\); \(\sqrt{196} = 14\); a diminution by a third is undone by an increase of a half, \(14 + 7 = 21\); \(21 \times 7 = 147\); an increase by three-quarters is undone by a diminution of three-sevenths, \(147 - 63 = 84\); \(84 \div 3 = 28\). Check. \(28 \times 3 = 84\); \(84 + 63 = 147\); \(147 \div 7 = 21\); \(21 - 7 = 14\); \(14^2 = 196\); \(196 - 52 = 144\); \(\sqrt{144} = 12\); \(12 + 8 = 20\); \(20 \div 10 = 2\).

docs.title: 10.5.2 Supposition
docs.text:
The method of supposition (iṣṭakarman), already met in the Bakhshālī manuscript (Section 10.2), handles problems in which the conditions are all proportional to the unknown: a number multiplied, divided, increased by fractions of itself and so on, with a final result given. Any convenient number is assumed and put through the conditions; the true number is then the assumed number multiplied by the given result and divided by the result obtained from the assumption.

Worked example: supposition

A number is multiplied by 5; a third of the product is subtracted; the remainder is divided by 10; and a third, a half and a quarter of the original number are added. The result is 68. What is the number? (Colebrooke 1817) Assume 3. Then \(3 \times 5 = 15\); \(15 - 5 = 10\); \(10 \div 10 = 1\); \(1 + 1 + \tfrac32 + \tfrac34 = 4\tfrac14\). The true result is 68, so the number is \(3 \times 68 \div 4\tfrac14 = 48\). Check. \(48 \times 5 = 240\); \(240 - 80 = 160\); \(160 \div 10 = 16\); \(16 + 16 + 24 + 12 = 68\).

Supposition fails when the conditions include a constant term or a square, since the result is then no longer proportional to the unknown. The texts know this: problems with added constants are solved by inversion, and those with squares and roots by special rules such as Mahāvīra’s rules for the “root” type (Section 10.4).

docs.title: 10.5.3 Concurrence and the dissimilar operation
docs.text:
Two short rules complete the set. “Concurrence” (saṅkramaṇa) finds two numbers from their sum and their difference: half the sum of the two given quantities is the larger number, half their difference the smaller. The “dissimilar operation” (viṣamakarman) finds two numbers from the difference of their squares and their simple difference: dividing the first by the second gives their sum, and the problem is reduced to concurrence. Both rest on simple identities, the second on \(a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)\).

Worked example: concurrence and the dissimilar operation

Concurrence. Two numbers have sum 101 and difference 25. The larger is \(\tfrac12(101 + 25) = 63\) and the smaller \(\tfrac12(101 - 25) = 38\). Dissimilar operation. The squares of two numbers differ by 40, and the numbers themselves by 4. Their sum is \(40 \div 4 = 10\), so by concurrence they are \(\tfrac12(10 + 4) = 7\) and \(\tfrac12(10 - 4) = 3\). Check: \(49 - 9 = 40\).

These methods are local: each applies to one shape of problem. The algebra of Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II (Chapters 4 and 9) replaced them with a single procedure: name the unknown, write the conditions as an equation, and solve it. The arithmetic books nevertheless kept them, because they were quick, easy to remember and well suited to mental calculation.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Śrīpati’s Gaṇitatilaka
docs.text: Śrīpati, an astronomer of the eleventh century (his Dhīkoṭidakaraṇa has the epoch 1039), wrote an arithmetic, the Gaṇitatilaka (“Ornament of calculation”), as well as the astronomical Siddhāntaśekhara, whose chapters on arithmetic and algebra overlap with it. The Gaṇitatilaka survives incomplete. It is of interest partly for its clear and orderly rules and partly for its commentary, written in the thirteenth century by the Jain monk Siṃhatilaka Sūri, which supplies worked solutions; the book thus shows a Brahmin astronomer’s arithmetic being taught in a Jain setting. H. R. Kapadia edited the text with Siṃhatilaka’s commentary in 1937 (Kapadia 1937; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 10.6.2 The Līlāvatī
docs.text: Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī (1150), described in Chapter 5, gathered the material of the earlier arithmetic books into a single, elegant text, and from the thirteenth century onward it displaced them over most of India. Its success shows the strengths of the genre: a fixed syllabus, rules short enough to memorise, examples that teach as they please, and commentaries that explain the reasons. Of the dozens of commentaries on it, those of Gaṇeśa Daivajña (1545) and of the Kerala school (Chapter 6) are the best known, and it was translated into Persian in 1587 (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 10.6.3 Nārāyaṇa’s Gaṇitakaumudī
docs.text:
The last major Sanskrit arithmetic book is the Gaṇitakaumudī (“Moonlight of calculation”) of Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita, completed in 1356. Its fourteen chapters begin with the usual operations and determinations, in a more expanded form than the Līlāvatī, and end with two chapters of original work on combinatorics and on magic squares (Chapter 8). Between them come chapters on topics the earlier books had treated briefly or not at all, among them the square-nature equation and the decomposition of fractions. Nārāyaṇa also gives a rule for finding the factors of a number by writing it as the difference of two squares, the method later associated in Europe with Fermat (Plofker 2009; Kusuba 2004).

Worked example: factors from a difference of squares

To factorise \(N = 2021\): the smallest square larger than \(N\) is \(45^2 = 2025\), and \(2025 - 2021 = 4 = 2^2\). Hence

\[2021 = 45^2 - 2^2 = (45 - 2)(45 + 2) = 43 \times 47 .\]

If the first difference is not a square, one tries \(46^2 - N\), \(47^2 - N\) and so on. The method is quickest when \(N\) has two factors close to each other, since then \(N\) lies just below a square.

docs.text:

docs.title: 10.7 Shared Problems: The Arithmetic Books in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Many problems in the Indian arithmetic books have close relatives in other traditions. The broken bamboo whose tip touches the ground, the reed or lotus in a pond, the channels filling a cistern and the purchase of a hundred birds for a hundred coins all appear in the Chinese Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art or its successors; problems in which given fractions of a whole and a known remainder determine the whole are found in Egyptian papyri and in the Greek epigrams collected in the Greek Anthology; and the “hundred animals” type appears in Latin in the collection of problems attributed to Alcuin of York (c. 800). Table 10.3 lists some of these parallels (Katz 2009; Plofker 2009; Joseph 2011).

Table 10.3. Some problem types shared by the Indian arithmetic books and other traditions Problem type Indian examples Elsewhere False position Bakhshālī manuscript; iṣṭakarman in the Līlāvatī Rhind papyrus (Egypt, c. 1550 BCE); “excess and deficit” in the Nine Chapters Fractions of a whole with a remainder Mahāvīra’s prakīrṇaka; the Līlāvatī’s bees Greek Anthology, book 14; medieval European collections Broken bamboo; reed in a pond Līlāvatī Nine Chapters, chapter 9 Channels filling a cistern Mahāvīra; Līlāvatī Nine Chapters; Greek Anthology A hundred birds for a hundred coins Mahāvīra’s “curious pulveriser” Zhang Qiujian (5th c.); Alcuin (c. 800); Abū Kāmil Travellers in progression Bakhshālī manuscript; Mahāvīra Nine Chapters; Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci

Such parallels raise the question of transmission, and it cannot usually be answered. Some problems were natural to any society that traded, built and taxed: a merchant anywhere might ask how long several channels take to fill a tank. Others are so specific in their form—the hundred birds, the broken bamboo with its particular geometry—that independent invention seems less likely than travel along the trade routes, by word of mouth among merchants as much as in books. But the routes, the dates and even the directions of travel are unknown, and the earliest surviving version of a problem is not necessarily the original. Historians of recreational mathematics have therefore learned to speak of a shared stock of problems circulating across Eurasia, to which India contributed and from which it drew, rather than of borrowing by one tradition from another.

What was distinctive in the Indian books was not the problems themselves but their treatment. Each problem type was tied to a named rule stated in general form, the rules were arranged in a fixed syllabus, and the examples were composed as poetry to be remembered. When Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci (1202) brought the Indian numerals to Italian merchants, it also brought many problems of the kinds described in this chapter, received through Arabic sources; how many of them were Indian in origin cannot now be determined.

docs.title: 10.8 Assessment
docs.text: The arithmetic books are the part of Indian mathematics that touched the largest number of people. Their rules for fractions, proportion, interest and mensuration were learned far more widely than the sine table or the cyclic method, and many of their procedures survived in the village schools into the nineteenth century (Chapter 13). Their methods were local rather than general: a separate rule for each type of problem, where a modern text would use one equation. But the classification of problem types was itself a form of analysis, and the best of the books—Mahāvīra’s above all—show a real interest in mathematical structure for its own sake, in unit fractions, combinations, series and “necklace” numbers. The verification of results, documented from the Bakhshālī manuscript onward, shows that the authors cared not only that a rule worked but that its answers could be checked.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Solve by false position: a man gives away a fifth of his money, then a quarter of the remainder, then a third of what is left, and has 12 left. How much had he at first?

  2. Reduce to a single fraction: a third increased by its own half, and the result diminished by its own quarter.

  3. Write \(\tfrac{5}{6}\) and \(\tfrac{4}{13}\) as sums of unit fractions by repeatedly taking the largest unit fraction that is not too large.

  4. Using Śrīdhara’s rule, find the volume of a sphere of diameter 6, and compare it with the exact value.

  5. Of a swarm of bees, a third and three times the square root of the swarm flew away, and 27 remained. How many bees were there?

  6. Factorise 5767 by writing it as a difference of two squares.

  7. Verify that \(27994681 \times 441 = 12345654321\), and explain why Mahāvīra might call such a product a “necklace”.

  8. Write 1 as a sum of four unit fractions using Mahāvīra’s rule.

Answers. (1) Assume 60: after the gifts \(60 \to 48 \to 36 \to 24\), so 24 would remain; the true remainder is 12, so the amount was \(60 \times 12/24 = 30\). (2) \(\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac32 = \tfrac12\), then \(\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac34 = \tfrac38\). (3) \(\tfrac56 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac13\); \(\tfrac{4}{13} = \tfrac14 + \tfrac{1}{18} + \tfrac{1}{468}\). (4) \(\tfrac{19}{36} \cdot 216 = 114\); exact value \(36\pi \approx 113.10\). (5) With \(x = y^2\): \(\tfrac23 y^2 - 3y - 27 = 0\), so by the rule \(y = \bigl(\tfrac32 + \sqrt{\tfrac94 + 18}\bigr)\big/\tfrac23 = (1.5 + 4.5) \times 1.5 = 9\), and the swarm had 81 bees. Check: \(27 + 27 = 54\) flew away and 27 remained. (6) \(76^2 = 5776\) and \(5776 - 5767 = 9 = 3^2\), so \(5767 = 73 \times 79\). (7) The product reads the same forwards and backwards, rising and falling like the beads of a necklace. (8) \(\frac12 + \frac13 + \frac19 + \frac1{18}\).

Scholarly Note: Further reading

Datta and Singh (1935–38), Part I, on arithmetic; Plofker (2009), chapters 4 and 6; Shukla (1959) for Śrīdhara’s Pāṭīgaṇita; Rangācārya (1912) for the Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha; Hayashi (1995) and Kaye (1927–33) for the Bakhshālī manuscript, with Plofker et al. (2017) on its dating; Kusuba (2004) on unit fractions; Kapadia (1937) for the Gaṇitatilaka (Datta and Singh 1935; Plofker 2009; Shukla 1959; Rangācārya 1912; Hayashi 1995; Kaye 1927; Plofker et al. 2017; Kusuba 2004; Kapadia 1937).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Mathematics at Work: Trade, Building and Surveying
docs.text: The arithmetic books described in Chapter 10 were written for people who had to calculate for a living. Their “determinations” (vyavahāra) turn the operations of arithmetic into procedures for particular trades: the merchant’s proportion and interest, the partner’s share of a profit, the goldsmith’s alloys, the overseer’s wages, the mason’s bricks, the sawyer’s cuts and the surveyor’s fields. This chapter follows those procedures through the texts of Śrīdhara, Mahāvīra and Bhāskara II, with worked examples. It asks also what the problems reveal about the economy they served. The institutions of trade, banking and credit are treated in Volume 19 of this series, Vāṇijya and Samudra, and the practice of architecture in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; here the subject is the mathematics (Plofker 2009; Datta and Singh 1935).

docs.title: 11.1.1 The rule of three
docs.text:
No rule was used more often than the rule of three (trairāśika, “the three quantities”). It is stated in a single verse by Āryabhaṭa (Chapter 3) and in every later arithmetic; Bhāskara II’s praise of it was quoted in Chapter 1. The three given quantities have fixed names. The “measure” (pramāṇa) is a known quantity and the “fruit” (phala) is what corresponds to it; the “requisition” (icchā) is the quantity for which a corresponding fruit, the “fruit of the requisition” (icchāphala), is sought. The terms are written in a row in the order measure, fruit, requisition. The first and last must be of the same kind (sajāti), and the answer is the fruit multiplied by the requisition and divided by the measure:

\[\text{}\mathit{icchāphala}\text{} = \frac{\text{}\mathit{phala}\text{} \times \text{}\mathit{icchā}\text{}}{\text{}\mathit{pramāṇa}\text{}} .\]

The rule needs no justification beyond proportion, and the texts give none. Its power lay in the discipline of setting the terms down in the right places, which turned a wide range of everyday questions into a single routine.

Worked example: the rule of three

If 6 measures of rice cost 45 paṇas, what do 14 measures cost? Measure 6, fruit 45, requisition 14:

\[\frac{45 \times 14}{6} = 105 \text{ }\mathit{paṇa}\text{s.}\]

The same layout serves an astronomer: if a planet makes a given number of revolutions in the civil days of a yuga, how many does it make in the days elapsed since the epoch? (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 11.1.2 The inverse rule
docs.text:
When the fruit decreases as the requisition increases, the “inverse rule of three” (vyastatrairāśika) applies: the answer is the fruit multiplied by the measure and divided by the requisition. The texts give a standard list of cases. The price of living beings—slaves, cattle, horses—was assumed to fall as their age rose beyond youth. The weight of gold needed to equal a given value rises as its fineness falls. And the number of measures in a heap of grain falls as the size of the measure rises. Bhāskara II’s example prices a female slave by her age: if one of sixteen years fetches 32 niṣkas, one of twenty fetches \(32 \times 16/20 = 25\tfrac35\) (Colebrooke 1817). The example is a plain reminder that slavery was part of the economy these books served, and that the arithmetic of the market applied to human beings as to other goods; the legal and social side of the matter is treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra.

Worked example: the inverse rule

A heap of grain measures 120 when measured with a vessel holding 7 units. How many times will a vessel holding 8 units be filled? The larger the vessel, the fewer the fillings:

\[\frac{120 \times 7}{8} = 105 .\]

docs.title: 11.1.3 Compound proportion
docs.text:
Many questions involve more than one ratio: the interest on a sum depends on both the principal and the time, the price of cloth on the number of pieces, their length and their breadth. Indian arithmetic handled these by the “rule of five” (pañcarāśika), “of seven” (saptarāśika), “of nine” (navarāśika) and so on, always with an odd number of terms. The data are written in two columns, one for the known case and one for the case sought, with the fruit at the foot of the known column. The fruit is then moved to the other column (“transposition of the fruits”), and the product of the column with more terms is divided by the product of the column with fewer. The procedure is a mechanical form of the reasoning that the answer is proportional to each factor in turn (Sarma 2002; Shukla 1959).

Worked example: the rule of seven

If 3 pieces of cloth, each 8 cubits long and 2 cubits wide, cost 60 paṇas, what do 5 pieces, each 12 cubits long and 3 cubits wide, cost?

Known case Case sought pieces 3 5 length 8 12 breadth 2 3 price 60 —

Moving the price to the second column, the answer is

\[\frac{5 \times 12 \times 3 \times 60}{3 \times 8 \times 2} = \frac{10800}{48} = 225 \text{ }\mathit{paṇa}\text{s}.\]

docs.title: 11.1.4 Barter
docs.text:
Barter (bhāṇḍapratibhāṇḍa, “goods for goods”) is treated as a special case of compound proportion. Two commodities have known prices in money, and the question is how much of one should be exchanged for a given quantity of the other. The money cancels out, and the rule of five gives the answer directly.

Worked example: barter

Mangoes sell at 3 for one paṇa, and pomegranates at 5 for two paṇas. How many pomegranates should be given for 30 mangoes? Thirty mangoes are worth \(30/3 = 10\) paṇas, which buy \(10 \times \tfrac52 = 25\) pomegranates. In the form of the rule of five:

\[\frac{30 \times 1 \times 5}{3 \times 2} = 25 .\]

docs.title: 11.1.5 The travels of the rule
docs.text: The rule of three is found in the Chinese Nine Chapters and in Indian texts from Āryabhaṭa onward; it may have been found independently in both. The Indian form, with its named terms and its extension to five, seven and more quantities, passed to the Islamic world: al-Bīrūnī wrote a treatise on the Indian rules of proportion, and the Arabic and Persian arithmetics treated the rule of three as a basic method. From them it reached medieval Europe, where merchant arithmetics called it the “golden rule” and taught it, together with the rules of five and seven, until the nineteenth century. S. R. Sarma has traced the Indian versions and their variants in detail (Sarma 2002; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 11.2.1 Terms and rates
docs.text:
The arithmetic books use a small vocabulary for loans. The principal is the “root” (mūla), the interest the “growth” (vṛddhi) or “increase over time” (kalāntara), and the principal and interest together the “mixture” (miśra). Rates are stated as so much on a hundred for a month—“five on a hundred each month”—and problems are solved with the rule of five, the five known quantities being the principal, time and interest of the stated rate and the principal and time of the case sought. Rates of this size (5 per cent a month is 60 per cent a year) look high to a modern reader, but they are typical of the problem collections, which were not concerned with the rates actually charged in any one market.

The legal texts also fixed rates. The Manusmṛti, for example, allows monthly interest of two, three, four and five per hundred according to the borrower’s varṇa, in descending order of rank (8.142), so that the lower the borrower’s status, the higher the lawful rate. The arithmetic books do not discuss the law; their rates are those convenient for calculation. The history of credit and of the regulation of interest is treated in Volumes 18 and 19.

Given any three of principal, rate, time and interest, the fourth follows by proportion. The texts go further and pose problems in which the data are mixed: the principal and interest are known only in sum, or several sums lent at different rates are compared.

Worked example: principal from the “mixture”

A sum lent at 5 per hundred a month amounts, with its interest, to 900 paṇas after 10 months. What was the principal? In 10 months a principal of 100 earns 50, so 100 becomes 150. By the rule of three, the principal of 900 is \(100 \times 900 / 150 = 600\), and the interest is 300.

Worked example: equal amounts at different rates

A total of 1770 paṇas is divided into three parts, lent for 10 months at 2, 3 and 5 per hundred a month respectively. At the end, the three amounts (principal with interest) are equal. Find the parts. In 10 months each 100 becomes 120, 130 and 150 respectively, so the parts must be proportional to \(\tfrac{1}{120} : \tfrac{1}{130} : \tfrac{1}{150}\), that is, to \(65 : 60 : 52\), whose sum is 177. The parts are therefore \(1770 \times \tfrac{65}{177} = 650\), \(600\) and \(520\). Check. \(650 \times 1.2 = 600 \times 1.3 = 520 \times 1.5 = 780\).

Problems of this second kind are a variant of the “proportional division” described below; Mahāvīra gives many of them, including problems in which the times differ instead of the rates. Interest on interest appears already in the Āryabhaṭīya (Chapter 3), where it leads to a quadratic equation. Instalment loans, in which a debt is paid off by equal payments at fixed intervals, also appear in the problem collections, though their treatment varies from author to author (Rangācārya 1912; Datta and Singh 1935).

docs.title: 11.3 Buying, Selling and Repayment
docs.text:
Problems of purchase and sale (krayavikraya) combine proportion with profit and loss. Goods are bought at one rate and sold at another, often with prices quoted as “so many for so much”—the commonest form of a price in a market without fixed units of packaging—and the question is the profit, the capital needed for a given profit, or the quantity to be traded. Such problems require the merchant to bring two rates to a common measure, which the rule of five does automatically.

Worked example: buying and selling at quoted rates

A merchant buys mangoes at 8 for 5 paṇas and sells them at 6 for 5 paṇas. How many must he trade to make a profit of 25 paṇas? One mango costs \(\tfrac58\) and sells for \(\tfrac56\), a profit of \(\tfrac56 - \tfrac58 = \tfrac{20 - 15}{24} = \tfrac{5}{24}\) paṇa each. A profit of 25 needs \(25 \div \tfrac{5}{24} = 120\) mangoes, bought for 75 and sold for 100 paṇas.

Money itself had to be converted. Coins of different issues, mints and weights circulated together, and their value depended on their metal content, not only on their names. Money-changers (Volume 19) exchanged them at a discount that reflected both the difference in fineness and their own charge. The arithmetic is a chain of proportions: the coins are first valued in a standard unit, and the changer’s commission is then deducted as a fraction of the result.

Worked example: exchanging coins

A trader brings 240 coins of an issue reckoned at \(\tfrac{15}{16}\) of the standard coin. The changer charges 1 in every 75 for the exchange. How many standard coins does the trader receive? The coins are worth \(240 \times \tfrac{15}{16} = 225\) standard coins; the commission is \(\tfrac{225}{75} = 3\); the trader receives 222.

Repayment of a debt by instalments that grow in a regular way leads to arithmetic progressions, and so to the rules for series. If the first payment and the increase are known, the number of payments needed to clear a given sum is the number of terms of a progression with that sum, found by Āryabhaṭa’s rule (Chapter 3). The same rules served for donations made on successive days of a festival, for the daily journeys of travellers and for courses of bricks that grow narrower towards the top of a stepped structure.

Worked example: payments in progression

A debt of 425 paṇas is repaid by monthly payments of 20 in the first month, 25 in the second, 30 in the third, and so on. How many months are needed? With first term \(a = 20\), difference \(d = 5\) and sum \(S = 425\), Āryabhaṭa’s rule gives

\[\begin{align*} n &= \frac12\left[\frac{\sqrt{8dS + (2a - d)^2} - 2a}{d} + 1\right] = \frac12\left[\frac{\sqrt{17000 + 1225} - 40}{5} + 1\right]\\ &= \frac12\left[\frac{135 - 40}{5} + 1\right] = 10 . \end{align*}\]

Check: the payments run from 20 to 65, and \(\tfrac{10}{2}(20 + 65) = 425\).

docs.title: 11.4 Partnership and Proportional Division
docs.text:
When several merchants pool their capital, the profit is divided in proportion to what each contributed. The rule is called prakṣepaka, from the word for a contribution or “throw-in”. The same rule divides an inheritance in given ratios, a wage among workers by the days each worked, or a cost among users in proportion to their use. When the contributions were made for different lengths of time, each is multiplied by its time before the division.

Worked example: partnership

Equal times. Three merchants contribute 40, 60 and 100 niṣkas, and the profit is 250. The shares are \(250 \times \tfrac{40}{200} = 50\), \(75\) and \(125\). Unequal times. Three partners contribute 40 for 12 months, 60 for 8 months and 100 for 3 months, and the profit is 420. The weighted contributions are \(480\), \(480\) and \(300\), with sum 1260, so the shares are \(420 \times \tfrac{480}{1260} = 160\), \(160\) and \(100\).

Proportional division was also the mathematics of distribution: of a king’s grant among the recipients, of grain among households, of a fine among offenders. The texts treat all these cases with the same rule.

docs.title: 11.5.1 The touch of gold
docs.text:
Gold was assayed by its “colour” or “touch” (varṇa), judged by rubbing it on a touchstone and comparing the streak with that of samples of known fineness. Pure gold had sixteen varṇas, and lower fineness was expressed as fewer varṇas; gold of 12 varṇas, on this scale, is three-quarters pure. The arithmetic books have a section on gold (suvarṇagaṇita) in which the touch of a mixture, the weight of an unknown component or the loss in refining is found. The mathematics is that of weighted averages, and the same rules apply to mixtures of grain or oil at different prices. The working practice of goldsmiths and assayers, and the treatises on the testing of coins and metals, are described in Volumes 14 (Rasāyana) and 17 (Śilpa–Kāru).

Worked example: the touch of an alloy

Ten māṣas of gold of 13 varṇas, 4 of 12 varṇas and 2 of 14 varṇas are melted together. What is the touch of the alloy? Multiply each weight by its touch and divide the sum by the total weight:

\[\frac{10\cdot 13 + 4\cdot 12 + 2\cdot 14}{10 + 4 + 2} = \frac{130 + 48 + 28}{16} = \frac{206}{16} = 12\tfrac78 \text{ }\mathit{varṇa}\text{s}.\]

Worked example: an unknown weight, and refining

Unknown weight. How much pure gold (16 varṇas) must be added to 12 māṣas of 10 varṇas to make gold of 12 varṇas? If \(x\) is added, \(12 \cdot 10 + 16x = 12(12 + x)\), so \(4x = 24\) and \(x = 6\). The texts state the rule without the unknown: the deficit of the base gold below the desired touch, multiplied by its weight, divided by the excess of the added gold over the desired touch, \(\tfrac{(12 - 10)\times 12}{16 - 12} = 6\). Refining. Twenty māṣas of gold of 12 varṇas are refined and weigh 16 māṣas afterwards. Since the amount of pure gold, \(20 \times 12\) in units of varṇa-weight, is unchanged, the new touch is \(240/16 = 15\) varṇas.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Combinations of goods
docs.text: The section on mixtures also contains the combinatorial problems mentioned in Chapter 10: how many different dishes can be made from six tastes taken one, two, three or more at a time; how many necklaces from gems of several kinds. These belong to the same practical world as the alloys—the cook’s and the jeweller’s—and they show the arithmetic books treating counting as one of the merchant’s tools (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 11.6 Work, Wages, Channels and Journeys
docs.text:
A group of problems concerns rates of work. Workers who complete a task in different times, channels that fill a tank at different rates, and travellers who move at different speeds are all treated by adding rates, not times. The “filling of a tank” (vāpīpūraṇa) is a standard example: if several channels, running alone, would fill a tank in given times, the fractions of the tank filled by each in a unit of time are added, and the reciprocal of the sum is the time taken by all together.

Worked example: channels and workers

Channels. Three channels would fill a tank in 3, 4 and 6 hours respectively. In one hour together they fill \(\tfrac13 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac34\) of the tank, so together they fill it in \(\tfrac43\) hours, that is 1 hour and 20 minutes. Workers. Five labourers dig a channel 40 cubits long in 8 days. How long will 4 labourers take to dig 60 cubits? The time varies inversely with the number of workers and directly with the length: \(8 \times \tfrac54 \times \tfrac{60}{40} = 15\) days. In the Indian layout this is a rule of five with the workers placed in the opposite columns.

Wage problems were often combined with partnership: when a team of workers of different skills is paid a lump sum, the payment is divided in proportion to each worker’s daily rate multiplied by the days worked. These problems give glimpses of the labour market, with its differential rates for skilled and unskilled work, although the numbers are those of the classroom, not of any one place and time.

docs.title: 11.7 Mensuration for Builders and Surveyors
docs.text: The rules of plane and solid mensuration were collected in Chapter 9 (Table 9.3). The arithmetic books give these rules a practical setting. They distinguish “practical” or “gross” rules, good enough for the field and easy to apply, from “accurate” rules, and they sometimes give both for the same figure. The pairing is instructive: it shows that the authors knew the gross rules to be approximate, and it lets us see the trade-off they made between simplicity and accuracy.

docs.title: 11.7.1 Fields
docs.text:
For a quadrilateral field the gross rule multiplies the half-sums of opposite sides. This is the “surveyor’s rule” found in many ancient and medieval traditions, from Mesopotamia and Egypt to the Roman land surveyors; it is exact for a rectangle and too large for every other quadrilateral. Brahmagupta’s accurate rule, \(\sqrt{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)(s-d)}\), is exact for a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle (Chapter 4); Bhāskara II warned that for other quadrilaterals the sides alone do not fix the area, so that a diagonal or a perpendicular must also be measured (Chapter 5).

Worked example: the gross and accurate areas of a field

A field is a trapezium with parallel sides of 12 and 8 rods and the other two sides each 5 rods. Gross rule. \(\tfrac{12 + 8}{2} \times \tfrac{5 + 5}{2} = 10 \times 5 = 50\) square rods. Accurate rule. The trapezium is symmetrical, and so can be inscribed in a circle. With \(s = \tfrac12(12 + 8 + 5 + 5) = 15\), Brahmagupta’s rule gives \(\sqrt{3 \cdot 7 \cdot 10 \cdot 10} = \sqrt{2100} \approx 45.83\) square rods. Check. The height of the trapezium is \(\sqrt{5^2 - 2^2} = \sqrt{21} \approx 4.583\), and its area is \(10 \times 4.583 = 45.83\). The gross rule is about 9% too large.

In practice, land was often measured by quantities other than area. Copper-plate grants of the Gupta period and later from Bengal, for example, measure land in kulyavāpas and droṇavāpas, units defined by the quantity of seed needed to sow it. Elsewhere, standard rods and ropes of locally defined length were used. The texts’ rules of mensuration had to be applied within these systems of measure, whose values varied from place to place (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 11.7.2 Excavations
docs.text:
A pit, a tank or a foundation trench whose top and bottom are rectangles of different sizes has the shape of a frustum. Brahmagupta computed its volume in three steps. The “practical” volume \(V_p\) is found from the mean dimensions: the average of the top and bottom lengths times the average of the widths, times the depth. The “gross” volume \(V_g\) is the average of the top and bottom areas times the depth. The “accurate” volume is then

\[V = V_p + \frac{V_g - V_p}{3} .\]

Mahāvīra gives the same procedure, with his own names for the two preliminary volumes. The result is exact, as the following example shows. Bhāskara II’s single formula for the same volume was given in Chapter 5 (Colebrooke 1817; Rangācārya 1912; Sarasvati Amma 1979).

Worked example: a tank with sloping sides

A tank is square, 10 cubits on a side at the top and 6 at the bottom, and 3 cubits deep. Practical volume. The mean side is 8, so \(V_p = 8^2 \times 3 = 192\). Gross volume. The mean area is \(\tfrac12(100 + 36) = 68\), so \(V_g = 68 \times 3 = 204\). Accurate volume. \(V = 192 + \tfrac{204 - 192}{3} = 196\) cubic cubits. Check. The exact volume of the frustum is \(\tfrac{h}{3}(a^2 + ab + b^2) = 1 \times (100 + 60 + 36) = 196\). In general \(V_p + \tfrac13(V_g - V_p) = \tfrac13(2V_p + V_g)\), and expanding \(2\left(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{a^2 + b^2}{2}\) gives \(a^2 + ab + b^2\), so the rule is exact for every such frustum.

For a pit of irregular depth the texts take the average of the depths measured at several places and multiply it by the area: a gross rule, but a sensible one. Wells were computed as cylinders, with the area of the circular section found by whatever value of the ratio of circumference to diameter the author used.

Worked example: a well

A circular well has a diameter of 4 cubits and a depth of 10 cubits. Its volume is the area of the circle times the depth. With the circumference taken as three times the diameter, the area is \(\tfrac14 \times 12 \times 4 = 12\) and the volume 120 cubic cubits; with \(\sqrt{10}\) the volume is \(10\sqrt{10} \times 4 \approx 126.5\); the true volume is \(40\pi \approx 125.7\). The “gross” value is about 4.5% too small, the Jain value about 0.7% too large.

docs.title: 11.7.3 Bricks and stones
docs.text:
The section on piles (citi) computes the number of bricks in a wall or platform: the volume of the structure divided by the volume of one brick. The number of courses is the height divided by the thickness of a brick. The rules are trivial in themselves; what they show is the use of arithmetic in planning and costing a building, a theme that the vāstu texts confirm (Volume 16).

Worked example: a brick wall

A wall is 20 cubits long, \(1\tfrac12\) cubits thick and 6 cubits high. Each brick measures 1 cubit by \(\tfrac12\) cubit by \(\tfrac14\) cubit. The wall contains \(20 \times 1\tfrac12 \times 6 = 180\) cubic cubits, and each brick \(\tfrac18\) cubic cubit, so \(180 \times 8 = 1440\) bricks are needed, laid in \(6 \div \tfrac14 = 24\) courses of 60 bricks each.

docs.title: 11.7.4 Sawing
docs.text:
The sawyer was paid by the area of the cuts he made (Chapter 4): each lengthwise cut through a log has an area equal to the length of the log times its thickness, and the total area is that of one cut times the number of cuts. A rate per unit of area then gives the wage by the rule of three. For a log that tapers, the thickness is averaged.

Worked example: the sawyer’s wage

A log 16 cubits long and \(1\tfrac12\) cubits thick is to be cut lengthwise into six planks. Five cuts are needed, each of area \(16 \times 1\tfrac12 = 24\) square cubits, so the total is 120 square cubits. If the rate is 2 paṇas for every 8 square cubits, the wage is \(120 \times \tfrac28 = 30\) paṇas.

docs.title: 11.7.5 Heaps against walls and in corners
docs.text:
The rule for a conical heap of grain on open ground, \((C/6)^2 h\) for circumference \(C\) and height \(h\), was given in Chapter 4. Grain was often heaped against a wall or in the corner of a storeroom, so that only part of the base circumference could be measured. The texts handle these cases by completing the heap in imagination. For a heap against a wall the measured arc is half the full circumference: the arc is doubled, the volume of the full heap is computed, and the result is halved. A heap in an inside corner is a quarter of a full heap, and one around an outside corner three-quarters, with the arc multiplied by four, or by four-thirds, accordingly.

Worked example: a heap in a corner

A heap of grain stands in the inside corner of a storeroom. Its curved edge measures 15 cubits and its height is 4 cubits. The full heap would have a circumference of \(4 \times 15 = 60\) and a volume of \((60/6)^2 \times 4 = 400\) cubic cubits; the heap in the corner is a quarter of this, 100 cubic cubits. The same reasoning gives, for an arc \(c\) against a wall, \(\tfrac12 (2c/6)^2 h = c^2 h/18\), and for an arc \(c\) in an inside corner, \(\tfrac14 (4c/6)^2 h = c^2 h/9\).

docs.title: 11.7.6 Heights and distances
docs.text: Shadows and gnomons (chāyā) form the last determination. Their mathematics—similar triangles—was described in Chapters 3 and 9, and their use in astronomy and in the orientation of buildings belongs to Volumes 12 and 16. The astronomers also described simple sighting instruments; Bhāskara II’s “instrument of the intellect” (dhīyantra), a graduated staff used to find the height and distance of an object from a single position, is described in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa. In the arithmetic books the shadow problems are mostly exercises in proportion: a lamp, a gnomon and its shadow; two gnomons and their shadows; the height of a tree from the length of its shadow and that of a staff.

docs.title: 11.8 How Accurate Were the Practical Rules?
docs.text:
Because the texts so often give a “gross” and an “accurate” rule side by side, it is possible to ask how large the errors of the gross rules were, and whether they mattered for the purposes in hand. Table 11.1 collects the examples worked in this chapter and in earlier ones, with the error of each rule computed against the exact value.

Table 11.1. Errors of some practical rules, computed for the examples in this volume Rule Example Error Circumference \(= 3 \times\) diameter any circle \(-4.5\%\) Circumference \(= \sqrt{10} \times\) diameter (Jain; Brahmagupta’s “accurate”) any circle \(+0.66\%\) Āryabhaṭa’s \(\pi \approx 3.1416\) any circle \(+0.0002\%\) Arc of a segment \(\approx \sqrt{6h^2 + c^2}\) (Jain) \(d = 10\), \(h = 2\) (Chapter 2) \(+1.2\%\) Quadrilateral: product of half-sums of opposite sides trapezium 12, 8, 5, 5 \(+9.1\%\) Frustum: “practical” volume from mean sides top 10, bottom 6, depth 3 \(-2.0\%\) Frustum: “gross” volume from mean areas same \(+4.1\%\) Conical heap: \((C/6)^2 h\) any cone \(+4.7\%\) Oval perimeter \(\approx \sqrt{6B^2 + 4L^2}\) (Mahāvīra) ellipse \(10 \times 6\) (Chapter 10) \(-2.8\%\)

Three points stand out. First, the gross rules were wrong by a few per cent, an error comparable to the uncertainty of measuring a field with a rope or the depth of a pit with a rod, and smaller than the variation between local units of measure; for most practical purposes they were adequate. Second, the two gross rules for the frustum err in opposite directions, and Brahmagupta’s accurate rule combines them in exactly the proportion that cancels the errors. It is hard to believe that this was found by chance, although the texts do not say how it was found. Third, the largest error in the table is that of the surveyor’s rule for quadrilaterals, which systematically overstates the area of any field that is not a rectangle. Where land was taxed by area, such an error had economic consequences, whichever party it favoured; Bhāskara II’s warning that the area of a quadrilateral cannot be found from its sides alone shows that the mathematicians, at least, were aware of the problem.

docs.title: 11.9 What the Problems Reveal
docs.text:
Read together, the determinations give a picture of the economy that the arithmetic books served—a picture that is real but must be read with care. The commodities are those of a commercial society: rice and other grain, cloth, spices and perfumes, gold, gems, horses, elephants, cattle and slaves. Money is used everywhere, in a hierarchy of units from the cowrie to the gold niṣka (Chapter 1), and credit at interest is taken for granted. Partnerships, wage labour and contract work for building and sawing all appear. The texts thus confirm, from an unusual angle, what inscriptions and legal texts say about a monetised economy with merchants’ associations and moneylenders.

The limits of this evidence are equally clear. The numbers are chosen to make the arithmetic come out, not to record prices; the same problems pass from book to book across centuries and regions; and the poetic framing, with its kings and lovers, is literary. The problems tell us what kinds of calculation were expected of an educated man of affairs, not what any particular merchant paid. Women appear in them mostly as addressees or as figures in the stories, and the labourers, sawyers and slaves of the examples are objects of calculation, not its practitioners. The people who actually did most of this arithmetic—merchants’ clerks, village accountants, masons—learned it in the schools described in Chapter 13, and mostly in the regional languages.

docs.title: 11.10 Assessment
docs.text: The practical mathematics of the arithmetic books is not where Indian mathematics was most original; proportion, interest, alloys and areas were calculated in every literate commercial society. What is distinctive is the way the material was organised. Problems were sorted into named classes, each with a rule stated in memorable verse; the rule of three was extended in a uniform way to any number of terms; and gross and accurate rules were set side by side, so that a user could choose and a reader could see the difference. Some results, such as Brahmagupta’s accurate volume of a frustum and the treatment of heaps in corners, show care in turning geometry into usable procedure. This organisation travelled: the rules of proportion and the problem types of the Indian books passed to the Islamic world and, through it, to the merchant arithmetics of Europe.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. If 8 cubits of cloth cost 36 paṇas, what do 30 cubits cost?

  2. If 12 workers build a wall in 15 days, how long will 20 workers take?

  3. A principal of 400 is lent at 3 per hundred a month. After how many months will principal and interest together amount to 568?

  4. Two merchants contribute 120 for 5 months and 150 for 6 months. Divide a profit of 330 between them.

  5. How many māṣas of gold of 9 varṇas must be added to 8 māṣas of 15 varṇas to produce gold of 13 varṇas?

  6. A pit is 12 cubits square at the top and 8 at the bottom, and 6 cubits deep. Find its practical, gross and accurate volumes.

  7. A heap of grain against a wall has a curved edge of 18 cubits and a height of 3 cubits. Find its volume by the texts’ rule.

Answers. (1) \(36 \times 30/8 = 135\). (2) \(15 \times 12/20 = 9\) days. (3) The interest is 168; a month’s interest is 12, so 14 months. (4) Weighted contributions 600 and 900: shares 132 and 198. (5) \(x\) satisfies \(9x + 120 = 13(8 + x)\), so \(4x = 16\) and \(x = 4\). (6) Practical \(10^2 \times 6 = 600\); gross \(\tfrac12(144 + 64) \times 6 = 624\); accurate \(600 + 8 = 608\), which is the exact volume \(\tfrac63(144 + 96 + 64) = 608\). (7) \(18^2 \times 3/18 = 54\) cubic cubits.

Scholarly Note: Further reading

Sarma (2002) on the rule of three and its variants; Shukla (1959) for Śrīdhara’s determinations; Rangācārya (1912), chapters 5–8 of Mahāvīra; Colebrooke (1817) for the Līlāvatī; Datta and Singh (1935–38), Part I; Sarasvati Amma (1979) on mensuration (Sarma 2002; Shukla 1959; Rangācārya 1912; Colebrooke 1817; Datta and Singh 1935; Sarasvati Amma 1979).

docs.title: Chapter 12: Exchanges: India and the Mathematical Sciences of Other Cultures
docs.text: Mathematical knowledge travelled in both directions across the borders of India. Indian astronomy absorbed Mesopotamian and Hellenistic ideas in the early centuries CE and transformed them; Indian numerals, arithmetic and astronomy passed to the Islamic world in the eighth century and through it to Europe; Indian astronomy reached China and Southeast Asia; and from the fourteenth century Islamic astronomy and mathematics, and later European science, came to India in their turn, through the courts of the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals and the Rajput kings. This chapter surveys these exchanges, keeping to what the evidence shows (Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 12.1.1 Mesopotamia and the early calendar
docs.text: The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, the earliest Indian text on calendrical astronomy (probably composed in the last centuries BCE, although some scholars place it much earlier), describes a five-year cycle of 1830 days with 62 synodic months, and uses simple linear rules for the length of daylight. David Pingree argued that some of its methods resemble those of Mesopotamian astronomy; others have stressed its independence. The question is unresolved (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 12.1.2 Hellenistic astronomy and astrology
docs.text: The evidence for Greek influence in the early centuries CE is much clearer. The Yavanajātaka (“Horoscopy of the Greeks”), a Sanskrit verse version of a Greek astrological text, introduced the twelve signs of the zodiac, the planetary houses and a body of technical vocabulary borrowed from Greek: horā (Greek hōra), kendra (kentron, “centre”), liptā (leptē, “minute of arc”), drekkāṇa (dekanos) and the Greek names of the zodiacal signs. Varāhamihira’s Pañcasiddhāntikā (mid-6th century) summarises five astronomical systems current in his time, two of which, the Romaka and Pauliśa, show Hellenistic origins in their names and methods. From these sources Indian astronomers took the geometrical models of planetary motion with epicycles and eccentrics, the division of the circle into 360 degrees and 21,600 minutes, and the idea of computing positions from tables of a trigonometric function (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 12.1.3 From chords to sines
docs.text:
The clearest example of transformation is trigonometry. Hellenistic astronomers computed with the chord of an arc: Ptolemy’s Almagest (2nd century CE) tabulates chords for every half-degree in a circle of radius 60, in sexagesimal fractions. The Indian sine is half the chord of twice the arc, \(R\sin\theta = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{crd}(2\theta)\). G. J. Toomer argued that the lost chord table of Hipparchus (2nd century BCE) used intervals of \(7\tfrac12^\circ\) and a radius of 3438 units; if so, Āryabhaṭa’s table of sines at intervals of \(3\tfrac34^\circ\) with the same radius is exactly the table of half-chords derived from it. Whether or not this reconstruction is right, the Indian step of tabulating the half-chord directly, and of developing the cosine and versed sine alongside it, was a genuine simplification that became standard in later astronomy everywhere (Toomer 1973; Van Brummelen 2009; Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981).

Chord and sine

In a circle of radius \(R\), the chord of an arc \(2\theta\) is \(\mathrm{crd}(2\theta) = 2R\sin\theta\). With Ptolemy’s radius \(R = 60\), the chord of \(60^\circ\) is 60 (the side of the inscribed hexagon), and the sine of \(30^\circ\) is half of it, 30. With Varāhamihira’s radius \(R = 120\) the sine of \(30^\circ\) is 60; with Āryabhaṭa’s \(R = 3438\) it is 1719. Ptolemy’s value \(\pi \approx 3;8,30\) in sexagesimal notation is \(3 + \tfrac{8}{60} + \tfrac{30}{3600} = 3.14167\).

Indian astronomers did not simply copy these models. They replaced the chord by the sine, recast the parameters within their own cosmic time-cycles, developed new computational procedures, and over the following centuries made the subject their own. The relationship is one of transmission followed by independent development, much as Greek astronomy had itself drawn on Babylonian observations and methods.

docs.title: 12.2 From India to the Islamic World
12.2.1 Astronomy
docs.text:
Indian astronomy reached the Islamic world early. The Zīj al-Arkand, an Arabic astronomical table compiled in Sind in 735, was based on Brahmagupta’s Khaṇḍakhādyaka; its title is the Arabic form of ahargaṇa, the Indian count of days. Around 770–773, an embassy from Sind to the court of the caliph al-Manṣūr in Baghdad included an Indian astronomer, with whose help an astronomical work of the school of Brahmagupta was translated into Arabic. The resulting works of Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī and Yaʿqūb ibn Ṭāriq, known as the Zīj al-Sindhind (from siddhānta), survive only in fragments and quotations. Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī prepared his own Zīj al-Sindhind around 830, combining Indian methods and parameters with others; it survives in a Latin translation made by Adelard of Bath in 1126 from a Spanish revision (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

Through these works the Indian sine entered Islamic astronomy, and with it the word jība (Chapter 3). Indian astronomy also used tables of the shadow of a gnomon for given altitudes of the Sun, and the “shadow” function (the cotangent, in modern terms) became in Islamic astronomy one of the starting points for the tangent and cotangent functions. Islamic astronomers soon went further, under the influence of Ptolemy, whose works were translated in the ninth century, and through their own research: they introduced the tangent and other functions, proved the sine theorem for spherical triangles, and computed far more accurate tables. Indian elements were thus one important ingredient in a new synthesis, not its whole (Gutas 1998; Katz 2009).

docs.title: 12.2.2 Numerals and arithmetic
docs.text: The Indian numerals and their methods of calculation were adopted in Arabic arithmetic from the late eighth century, and Arabic authors consistently called them “Indian”: al-Khwārizmī’s book on “Indian reckoning” (c. 825), al-Uqlīdisī’s Chapters on Indian Arithmetic (952), and many later works (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 12.2.3 Algebra
docs.text: Whether Indian algebra influenced the algebra of al-Khwārizmī (c. 825), the first Arabic book on the subject, is uncertain. His work shares with Indian algebra the idea of a general procedure for solving quadratic equations, but it uses no negative numbers, has no symbolic notation, justifies its rules geometrically, and does not treat indeterminate equations. Historians have argued for Mesopotamian, Greek, Indian and Syriac contributions in various proportions. It is safest to say that al-Khwārizmī worked in a milieu in which Indian arithmetic and astronomy were well known, and that a direct debt to Brahmagupta’s algebra has not been demonstrated (Plofker 2009; Rosen 1831).

docs.title: 12.2.4 Al-Bīrūnī
docs.text: The most important Islamic student of Indian science was Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī (973–after 1050), who accompanied the campaigns of Maḥmūd of Ghazni into north-western India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote around 1030 a comprehensive account of Indian religion, philosophy and science, the Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind, translated into English by Edward Sachau in 1888 (al-Bīrūnī 1888). He described the Indian numerals and number names, the astronomical systems of Brahmagupta and others, and Indian measures of time and space, and he translated several Sanskrit works into Arabic. He was candid in criticism as well as in praise: he admired Indian astronomy but complained of the disorder of its texts and the reluctance of Indian scholars to share their knowledge with foreigners.

docs.title: 12.3.1 China
docs.text:
Indian astronomy reached Tang China with Buddhism. Several Indian astronomical families served at the Tang court, and in 718 Gautama Siddha (Qutan Xida) compiled the Jiuzhi li (“Navagraha calendar”), which is preserved in the Kaiyuan zhanjing. It describes Indian methods for computing the positions of the Sun and Moon, a table of sines, and the Indian numerals, including a dot for zero. Chinese astronomers did not adopt the sine table or the numerals; their own tradition of rod calculation was already positional and decimal, with a blank for zero (Plofker 2009). The Indian astronomers at the Tang court were nonetheless influential. Chinese records also report a quarrel: after the monk Yixing’s Dayan calendar was adopted in 729, a member of the Gautama family is said to have charged that it was copied from the Jiuzhi li, and the charge was rejected after the calendars had been compared.

Indian astronomy also reached China and Japan in Buddhist texts on astrology, such as the Xiuyao jing (8th century), which transmitted the Indian lunar mansions and planetary weekdays. These had a long life in East Asian calendrical and divinatory practice.

docs.title: 12.3.2 Tibet
docs.text: Indian calendrical astronomy was transmitted to Tibet especially through the Kālacakra Tantra (early 11th century), whose astronomical sections are the basis of the traditional Tibetan calendar.

docs.title: 12.3.3 Southeast Asia
docs.text: In Southeast Asia, kingdoms that used Sanskrit and Indian scripts also adopted Indian calendars and numerals. Inscriptions in Cambodia and Sumatra dated in the Śaka era use place-value numerals with zero from the 680s (Chapter 7). Later calendrical systems in Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos derive from Indian astronomy, in particular from the tradition of the Sūryasiddhānta; the Thai and Burmese calendars still use parameters of Indian origin.

docs.title: 12.4 From the Islamic World to India
docs.text:
From the fourteenth century, the flow of knowledge was reversed. Persian became the language of administration across much of India under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and Islamic astronomy and mathematics were studied at court and in the madrasa.

  • The astrolabe. Mahendra Sūri, a Jain scholar at the court of Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq in Delhi, wrote the Yantrarāja (1370), the first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe, an instrument developed in the Hellenistic and Islamic worlds.
